corp-cloud.title: Cloud computing: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud concepts
corp-cloud.description: Chapter-by-chapter cloud foundations mapped across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud: concepts, compute, storage and databases, networking, identity and security, cost and well-architected design — useful for AZ-900, AWS Cloud Practitioner and Google Cloud ACE style preparation.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Cloud concepts and global infrastructure
courses.summary: What makes something 'cloud', service models and the shared responsibility model, deployment models and cloud economics, and regions, availability zones and edge locations across the three big providers.
outcomes: Learners can list the five essential cloud characteristics
Learners can compare IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless and who secures what
Learners can explain public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud, and CapEx vs OpEx
Learners can explain regions, availability zones and edge locations

story.title: The server room in the basement

scenes.text: A Pune logistics firm buys servers every three years, guessing capacity. During Diwali they run out; in February half sit idle.
Moving to the cloud, they rent what they need by the hour and scale for the festival rush.

steps.title: NIST's five essential characteristics
steps.body:
The widely used NIST definition (SP 800-145) says cloud computing has:
- **On-demand self-service:** provision resources yourself, no human ticket.
- **Broad network access:** available over the network from many devices.
- **Resource pooling:** provider's resources shared across many customers (multi-tenancy).
- **Rapid elasticity:** scale out and in quickly, often automatically.
- **Measured service:** usage metered and billed (pay-as-you-go).

steps.title: Key benefits
steps.body: High availability, scalability, elasticity, agility (minutes not months), global reach, security tooling, and paying for what you use. **Scalability** = can handle more load by adding resources; **elasticity** = automatically adds *and removes* resources as demand changes.

steps.title: Solved example: which characteristic?
steps.body:
**a)** Developer launches a VM from a web console in 2 minutes → on-demand self-service.
**b)** Bill shows 312 VM-hours this month → measured service.
**c)** Web tier grows from 4 to 40 instances during a sale and back to 4 → rapid elasticity.

steps.title: About exam tags
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing scalability with elasticity (elasticity includes scaling *down* automatically).
- Thinking 'cloud' just means 'someone else's data centre' — the self-service, metered, elastic model is the point.

activity.prompt: Match the example to the NIST characteristic.
pairs: Launch a database from a console without calling anyone
Billing by the second for compute used
Automatically adding servers at peak and removing them later
Many customers share the provider's hardware securely
Access from laptop, phone and API over the internet

quiz.q: How many essential characteristics in the NIST definition?
quiz.why: The NIST definition lists five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

quiz.q: Elasticity differs from scalability because it:
options: Automatically scales up and down with demand
quiz.why: Elasticity means resources scale automatically both up and down with demand. Scalability alone may only mean the ability to grow.
Pay-as-you-go maps to measured service, because usage is metered and billed accordingly.
Multi-tenancy, where many customers share the same underlying resources, relates to resource pooling.
A key cloud benefit is agility, since resources can be provisioned in minutes. Fixed capacity, long procurement and upfront hardware purchase are traditional drawbacks.

lessons.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, serverless and shared responsibility

scenes.text: After a breach on a cloud VM, the team asks: 'Wasn't the provider supposed to patch that?'
The answer depends on the service model they chose.

steps.title: Service models
steps.body:
- **IaaS:** you get VMs, storage, networks; you manage OS, runtime, apps. (EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Compute Engine)
- **PaaS:** provider manages OS and runtime; you deploy code and data. (Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, App Engine)
- **SaaS:** complete application; you manage users, data and settings. (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce)
- **Serverless/FaaS:** run functions on events; no servers to manage; pay per execution. (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Run functions)

steps.title: Shared responsibility model
steps.body: The provider is always responsible for **physical data centres, hardware, network and the virtualisation layer** ('security **of** the cloud', in AWS's words). The customer is **always** responsible for **their data, identities/accounts, access management and devices**. In between, responsibility shifts: in IaaS you patch the OS; in PaaS the provider does; in SaaS the provider runs almost everything except your data, users and configuration.

steps.title: Solved example: who is responsible?
steps.body:
**a)** OS patch on an Azure VM → **customer** (IaaS).
**b)** OS patch for Azure App Service → **provider** (PaaS).
**c)** A user in Microsoft 365 with a weak password and no MFA → **customer** (identities are always yours).
**d)** Data-centre door security → **provider**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the provider secures your data configuration (e.g. a public storage bucket) — that's you.
- Thinking serverless means 'no responsibility' — code, permissions and data are still yours.

activity.prompt: Who is responsible in IaaS?

items.text: Guest operating system patching
Physical security of data centre
User accounts and MFA
Hypervisor and host hardware
Firewall rules on the VM's network
Classifying and protecting data

quiz.why: Azure App Service is PaaS, a managed platform where you deploy code without managing the servers or OS.
Data and identities are always the customer's responsibility in every service model. The provider handles data-centre power, hosts and the hypervisor.

quiz.q: Who patches the OS on an EC2 instance?
quiz.why: EC2 is IaaS, so the customer patches the guest OS. AWS looks after the hardware and hypervisor.
Microsoft 365 is a complete application delivered over the internet, which is SaaS.
AWS Lambda runs your code as serverless functions (FaaS). It is not a VM, database or CDN.

sources: AWS, Microsoft and Google shared responsibility documentation

scenes.text: A bank keeps its core ledger in its own data centre for regulatory reasons.
Its mobile app and analytics run in a public cloud, connected securely — a hybrid model.

steps.title: Deployment models
steps.body:
- **Public cloud:** provider-owned, shared infrastructure, accessed over the internet.
- **Private cloud:** cloud-style infrastructure used by one organisation (on-premises or hosted).
- **Hybrid cloud:** public + private connected, with workloads moving or integrating between them.
- **Multi-cloud:** using more than one public cloud provider.

steps.title: CapEx vs OpEx
steps.body:
- **CapEx (capital expenditure):** big upfront spend on physical assets (servers), depreciated over years.
- **OpEx (operational expenditure):** ongoing pay-for-use spending.
Public cloud moves IT mostly to **OpEx**. Providers' **economies of scale** let them offer lower unit prices.

steps.title: Solved example: compare costs
steps.body:
On-prem: ₹60 lakh servers (5-year life) + ₹8 lakh/year power & staff → per year ≈ ₹12 lakh + ₹8 lakh = **₹20 lakh/year** whether used or not.
Cloud: average 10 VMs × ₹9,000/month = ₹10.8 lakh/year, rising only in peak months.
**Insight:** cloud wins for variable load; steady 24×7 workloads may need reservations to compete.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming cloud is always cheaper — unmanaged sprawl can cost more.
- Calling 'two clouds' hybrid — hybrid means public + private; multiple publics = multi-cloud.

activity.prompt: Match the scenario to the deployment model.
pairs: Startup runs everything on one public provider
Bank: on-prem ledger + public cloud apps, connected
Company uses AWS for apps and Google Cloud for analytics
Government agency runs its own cloud platform in its data centre

quiz.why: Buying servers upfront is capital expenditure (CapEx), because they are capital assets. Cloud use is mostly OpEx.
Hybrid cloud combines public and private clouds, connected together.
Economies of scale let providers buy and run at large scale, so they can offer lower unit prices.
Multi-cloud means using more than one public cloud provider. Public plus private is hybrid.
Cloud spending is mostly OpEx, since you pay for what you use rather than buying assets.

lessons.title: Regions, availability zones and edge

scenes.text: Heavy rain floods one data centre in a city.
An app spread across three availability zones in that region keeps running.

steps.title: Regions
steps.body: A **region** is a geographic area with one or more data centres (e.g. Mumbai, Hyderabad, Pune/Central India, Chennai/South India — depending on provider). Choose by **latency to users, data-residency rules, service availability and price**.

steps.title: Availability zones
steps.body: An **availability zone (AZ)** is one or more physically separate data centres within a region, with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by low-latency links. Deploying across **multiple AZs** protects against a data-centre failure. AWS regions have multiple AZs (typically three or more); Azure regions that support AZs have at least three; Google Cloud regions have multiple **zones**.

steps.title: Provider-specific terms
steps.body:
- **Azure region pairs:** most Azure regions are paired with another region in the same geography for platform updates and some geo-replication.
- **Azure resource groups, subscriptions** organise resources (covered in Ch 5).
- **Edge locations / points of presence:** used by CDNs and DNS (CloudFront, Azure Front Door/CDN, Cloud CDN) to serve users nearby.

steps.title: Solved example: design for availability
steps.body:
**Need:** survive a data-centre outage for an Indian e-commerce app.
**Design:** web and app tiers in 3 AZs of an Indian region behind a load balancer; database with a synchronous standby in another AZ; daily backups copied to a second region for disaster recovery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting all VMs in one AZ 'for low latency' — a single failure takes everything down.
- Assuming every service exists in every region — check availability first.

activity.prompt: Order from largest to smallest scope.

options: Separate data centre(s) within a region
quiz.why: An availability zone is one or more separate data centres within a region, with independent power and networking.

options: A global outage of all providers
quiz.why: Spreading across AZs protects against a data-centre failure by isolating faults. It doesn't fix bad code or weak passwords.
Region choice depends on latency, data residency, available services and price. Logo colour or office size are irrelevant.

quiz.q: Edge locations are mainly used by:
quiz.why: Edge locations are mainly used by CDN and DNS services to serve content close to users.
Azure region pairs help with sequential platform updates and geo-redundancy, so a paired region is protected during updates and disasters.

sources: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud global infrastructure documentation

questions.q: Which is NOT a NIST essential characteristic?
questions.why: Fixed annual capacity is the opposite of the NIST characteristic of rapid elasticity. The others are genuine NIST characteristics.

questions.q: Google Workspace is:
questions.why: Google Workspace is a finished application delivered as a service, which is SaaS.

questions.q: Public + private connected =
questions.why: A public cloud connected with a private cloud or on-premises setup is a hybrid cloud.

questions.q: In PaaS, OS patching is done by:
questions.why: In PaaS the provider manages the OS and its patching. The customer manages the application and data.

questions.q: Cloud shifts spending mainly to:
questions.why: Cloud shifts spending mainly to OpEx because you pay as you go instead of buying hardware upfront.

questions.q: A region contains:
questions.why: A region contains availability zones, which are separate data centres. Users and subscriptions aren't part of a region's structure.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Customers are always responsible for their data. Reason (R): The shared responsibility model never transfers data ownership to the provider.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: under shared responsibility, data ownership never moves to the provider, so customers are always responsible for their data.

questions.q: Automatically removing servers after a peak demonstrates:
questions.why: Automatically removing servers after a peak is scaling in, a sign of elasticity.

questions.q: Using AWS and Azure together is:
questions.why: Using AWS and Azure together means using more than one public provider, which is multi-cloud.

questions.q: Which is the customer's job in SaaS?
questions.why: In SaaS the customer manages user access and their data. The provider handles servers, hypervisor and cooling.

questions.q: Case: A storage bucket was left public and data leaked. Who is responsible?
questions.why: A public storage bucket is a configuration choice, so the customer is responsible for the leak. The provider secures the platform, not your settings or data.

questions.q: Case: Steady 24×7 workload; cloud on-demand looks costlier than on-prem. Best lever?
options: Reservations/savings plans or committed use discounts
questions.why: For a steady 24×7 workload, commitment discounts like reservations, savings plans or committed use cut the cost versus on-demand.

questions.q: Case: Indian law requires certain data to stay in India. Which choice matters most?
questions.why: Data residency is controlled by region selection, so choose a region in India. Instance count and CDN don't set where data lives.

questions.q: Which design survives a single AZ failure?
options: Instances in 3 AZs behind a load balancer
One VM per region with no LB
questions.why: Instances in 3 AZs behind a load balancer keep serving if one AZ fails. Two VMs in one AZ or a single VM share a failure point.

questions.q: Which statement about serverless is MOST accurate?
options: It's always cheaper for any workload
There are no servers at all
Servers exist but are fully managed; you pay per execution and still own code, permissions and data
questions.why: Serverless still uses servers, but the provider manages them fully and you pay per execution. You still own code, permissions and data, and it isn't always cheaper.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Compute: VMs, containers, serverless and scaling
courses.summary: Virtual machines and pricing options, containers and Kubernetes, serverless functions, and autoscaling with load balancers — with the equivalent service names on each cloud.
outcomes: Learners can pick VM pricing models for different workloads
Learners can explain containers vs VMs and managed Kubernetes options
Learners can describe serverless trade-offs including cold starts and time limits
Learners can map autoscaling and load-balancing services across clouds

lessons.title: Virtual machines and pricing models

scenes.text: An animation studio needs 200 machines for 6 hours each night to render frames.
Using spare 'spot' capacity cuts the bill dramatically — because a render can restart if a machine is reclaimed.

steps.title: VM services
steps.body: **AWS EC2**, **Azure Virtual Machines**, **Google Compute Engine**. Choose an image (OS), a size/family (general purpose, compute-optimised, memory-optimised, GPU), disks, network and region/zone.

steps.title: Pricing models
steps.body:
- **On-demand / pay-as-you-go:** no commitment; highest unit price; flexible.
- **Reserved / savings plans / committed use discounts:** 1- or 3-year commitment for large discounts on steady workloads.
- **Spot (AWS, Azure) / Spot VMs (Google, formerly preemptible):** spare capacity at deep discounts, but can be **reclaimed** at short notice — only for interruptible work.
- **Dedicated hosts:** physical server for you (licensing/compliance).

steps.title: Solved example: match workload to pricing
steps.body:
**a)** Production database 24×7 for 3 years → **reserved/committed**.
**b)** Nightly render batch that can restart → **spot**.
**c)** Two-week hackathon environment → **on-demand**.
**d)** Software licensed per physical core → **dedicated host**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running stateful databases on spot.
- Oversized VMs 'just in case' — right-size using monitoring.
- Forgetting stopped VMs may still incur disk charges.

activity.prompt: Best pricing model?

items.text: Unpredictable new app for a month
ERP servers running 24×7 for years
Batch image processing that can retry
CI build agents that can be interrupted
Short demo environment
Steady web tier baseline

quiz.why: Spot capacity can be reclaimed at short notice, so it suits interruptible batch work. Databases, payment systems and domain controllers need to stay up.
Azure's VM service is Azure Virtual Machines. EC2 is AWS, Compute Engine is Google, and Lambda is AWS functions.
Reserved pricing suits steady, long-running workloads because you commit for 1 to 3 years in return for a discount.
Google's VM service is Compute Engine, which is IaaS.

options: Matching VM size to actual usage
quiz.why: Right-sizing means matching VM size to actual usage so you don't pay for unused capacity.

sources: AWS EC2, Azure VM and Compute Engine pricing documentation

scenes.text: An app runs on Neha's laptop but fails on the server because of a different library version.
Packaging it as a container image makes it run the same everywhere.

steps.title: Containers vs VMs
steps.body: A **VM** virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS. A **container** packages an app with its libraries and shares the host OS kernel — lighter, starts in seconds, many per host. Images are built once (e.g. with a Dockerfile) and run anywhere a container runtime exists.

steps.title: Kubernetes
steps.body: **Kubernetes** orchestrates containers: scheduling onto nodes, restarting failed containers, scaling replicas, rolling updates, service discovery and load balancing. Key objects: **Pod** (one or more containers), **Deployment** (desired replicas), **Service** (stable network endpoint).

steps.title: Managed options
steps.body:
- Managed Kubernetes: **Amazon EKS**, **Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)**, **Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)**.
- Simpler container services: **Amazon ECS** (with Fargate for serverless containers), **Azure Container Instances / Azure Container Apps**, **Google Cloud Run**.
- Image registries: **Amazon ECR**, **Azure Container Registry**, **Google Artifact Registry**.

steps.title: Solved example: choose a platform
steps.body:
**a)** One small API container, scale to zero when idle → Cloud Run / Azure Container Apps / ECS on Fargate.
**b)** 60 microservices, need custom networking and operators → managed Kubernetes (EKS/AKS/GKE).
**c)** Legacy Windows app needing full OS control → VM.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing Kubernetes for a single small app — operational overhead.
- Storing data inside containers — they're disposable; use volumes or managed databases.

activity.prompt: Match the service to its cloud.
pairs: Run single containers on Azure without managing servers

quiz.why: Containers share the host's OS kernel, which makes them lightweight compared with VMs that each have a full guest OS.
A Kubernetes Deployment defines the desired number of replicas of pods, and Kubernetes keeps that desired state.
Azure's managed Kubernetes service is AKS. EKS is AWS and GKE is Google.

options: Is lost when the container is replaced
quiz.why: A container's filesystem is ephemeral, so its data is lost when the container is replaced. Use persistent volumes for data that must last.

quiz.q: Best for one small API that scales to zero:
quiz.why: For one small API that scales to zero, serverless containers like Cloud Run are simplest. A large Kubernetes cluster or mainframe is overkill.

lessons.title: Serverless functions

scenes.text: Every time a user uploads a photo, a thumbnail must be made.
A function triggered by the storage event does it — and costs nothing when no one uploads.

steps.title: Function services
steps.body: **AWS Lambda**, **Azure Functions**, **Google Cloud Run functions** (formerly Cloud Functions). Code runs in response to **events** (HTTP request, file upload, queue message, schedule) and you pay per invocation and execution time.

steps.title: Trade-offs
steps.body:
**Pros:** no servers to manage, automatic scaling, pay per use, great for event-driven glue.
**Cons:** **cold starts** (first call after idle is slower), **execution time limits** (e.g. Lambda max 15 minutes per invocation), statelessness, vendor-specific triggers, harder local debugging.

steps.title: Solved example: cost intuition
steps.body: 1 million invocations/month, 200 ms each, 512 MB memory → 1,000,000 × 0.2 s × 0.5 GB = **100,000 GB-seconds**. Providers price per GB-second plus per request, often with a free tier — so small event workloads can be very cheap.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Long-running jobs (hours) on functions — use containers/batch.
- Storing state in function memory between calls.
- Giving functions broad permissions — grant least privilege.

activity.prompt: 2,000,000 invocations × 0.1 s × 1 GB memory = how many GB-seconds?

options: Extra latency when a function starts after being idle
quiz.why: A cold start is the extra latency when a function starts after being idle, because the environment must initialise.
AWS Lambda's maximum duration per invocation is 15 minutes.
Serverless billing is mainly by the number of invocations and execution time. There's no charge for idle servers.
Generating a thumbnail when a file is uploaded is short and event-driven, so it is a good serverless use case. Long encodes and databases are not.
Azure's function service is Azure Functions. Lambda is AWS and Cloud Run functions are Google.

sources: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Run functions documentation

lessons.title: Autoscaling and load balancing services

scenes.text: An exam board's results site expects 50× normal traffic for a few hours.
Scale sets behind a load balancer grow and shrink automatically.

steps.title: Autoscaling groups
steps.body:
- AWS **EC2 Auto Scaling groups**
- Azure **Virtual Machine Scale Sets**
- Google **Managed instance groups (MIGs)**
Define a template, min/max/desired counts, and scaling policies (CPU, requests, schedules). Unhealthy instances are replaced.

steps.title: Load balancers
steps.body:
- AWS **Elastic Load Balancing**: Application Load Balancer (L7), Network Load Balancer (L4), Gateway LB.
- Azure **Load Balancer** (L4), **Application Gateway** (L7, with WAF option), **Front Door** (global L7 + CDN).
- Google **Cloud Load Balancing** (global and regional, L4/L7).

steps.title: Solved example: results-day plan
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Scheduled scale-out to 40 instances an hour before release.
**Step 2:** Target-tracking policy keeps CPU ~60% up to max 120.
**Step 3:** L7 load balancer across 3 AZs with health checks.
**Step 4:** Static results pages cached at the CDN.
**Step 5:** Scale in after the peak.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Max count too low for the event.
- Health checks pointing to a page that doesn't test dependencies.
- Forgetting to load-test before the big day.

activity.prompt: Match the cloud service to its role.
pairs: Azure layer-7 load balancer with optional WAF

quiz.why: Azure's autoscaling VM feature is Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS). EC2 Auto Scaling is AWS and MIG is Google.

quiz.q: An L7 load balancer on AWS:
quiz.why: An L7 (HTTP-aware) load balancer on AWS is the Application Load Balancer. The Network Load Balancer works at layer 4.
Scheduled scaling is ideal for known events like results day, where demand is predictable. Random spikes need reactive autoscaling.
Autoscaling groups replace unhealthy instances, which makes them self-healing.

options: Global L7 load balancing and CDN
quiz.why: Azure Front Door provides global L7 load balancing and CDN as a global entry point. It isn't billing, block storage or VMs.

sources: Provider documentation on autoscaling and load balancing

questions.q: AWS VM service:
questions.why: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is AWS's VM service. S3 is storage, RDS is databases and IAM is identity.

questions.q: Spot VMs can be:
questions.why: Spot VMs use spare capacity and can be reclaimed at short notice. They aren't free or guaranteed.

questions.q: Containers vs VMs: containers are:
questions.why: Containers are lighter and start faster than VMs because they share the host kernel instead of running a full OS each.

questions.q: Google managed Kubernetes:
questions.why: Google's managed Kubernetes service is GKE. EKS is AWS, AKS is Azure and ECS is AWS containers.

questions.q: Serverless cold start affects:
questions.why: A serverless cold start affects latency after the function has been idle, because of initialisation time.

questions.q: Committed-use/reserved discounts need:
questions.why: Committed-use and reserved discounts need a 1- to 3-year commitment. Spot and on-demand have none.

questions.q: GB-seconds for 500,000 calls × 0.4 s × 0.5 GB:
questions.why: GB-seconds = calls × seconds × GB = 500,000 × 0.4 × 0.5 = 100,000.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Spot is suitable for a primary database. Reason (R): Spot capacity can be interrupted.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: spot capacity can be interrupted, so it is unsuitable for a primary database.

questions.q: Which runs a single container without managing servers on Azure?
questions.why: Azure Container Instances (ACI) runs a single container without managing servers. A VM requires you to manage the OS.

questions.q: Kubernetes Service object provides:
questions.why: A Kubernetes Service gives pods a stable network endpoint and handles discovery and load balancing, even as pods change.

questions.q: Case: A 3-hour video transcode keeps failing on Lambda. Why and fix?
questions.why: Lambda is limited to 15 minutes, so a 3-hour transcode fails. Use containers or a batch service for long jobs.

questions.q: Case: Web tier baseline 10 VMs always, spikes to 40 on sales. Cost-optimal mix?
options: Reserve baseline, autoscale on-demand (spot for tolerant parts)
questions.why: Reserve the steady baseline of 10 VMs, then autoscale on-demand for spikes, using spot for tolerant parts. Reserving 40 wastes money, and all on-demand costs more.

questions.q: Case: Results site crashes despite autoscaling; max set to 10. Fix?
questions.why: The autoscaling maximum of 10 is too low for the spike. Raise the maximum, pre-scale for known events and load test.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Azure Functions ↔ AWS Lambda ↔ Cloud Run functions
questions.why: Azure Functions, AWS Lambda and Cloud Run functions are the equivalent function (FaaS) services. The other pairings mix unrelated services.

questions.q: Why can containers start faster than VMs?
options: They are always cached in CDN
No guest OS boot — they reuse the host kernel
questions.why: Containers reuse the host kernel, so they skip booting a guest OS and start faster than VMs.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Storage and databases
courses.summary: Object, block and file storage; tiers, durability and redundancy options; managed relational databases; and NoSQL and analytics services across the three clouds.
outcomes: Learners can choose object, block or file storage
Learners can pick storage tiers and Azure redundancy options
Learners can map managed relational databases across clouds
Learners can map NoSQL and data-warehouse services

scenes.text: A media company has: VM boot disks, shared design files for 50 editors, and 2 PB of finished videos.
Each needs a different type of storage.

steps.title: Object storage
steps.body: Stores **objects** (file + metadata) in buckets/containers, accessed over HTTP APIs; virtually unlimited; great for media, backups, data lakes, static websites. **Amazon S3**, **Azure Blob Storage**, **Google Cloud Storage**.

steps.title: Block storage
steps.body: Raw disk volumes attached to a VM, low latency; for OS disks and databases. **Amazon EBS**, **Azure Managed Disks**, **Google Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk**.

steps.title: File storage
steps.body: Shared file systems (NFS/SMB) mounted by many machines. **Amazon EFS** (and FSx), **Azure Files**, **Google Filestore**.

steps.title: Solved example: the media company
steps.body: Boot disks → **block**. Shared design folders for 50 editors → **file** (SMB/NFS). 2 PB finished videos served to apps/CDN → **object**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using block storage for a shared drive (most block volumes attach to one VM at a time).
- Making buckets public by accident — block public access by default.

activity.prompt: Which storage type?

items.text: Database data volume on a VM
Backups and archives
Shared team drive mounted over SMB
Images for a website served via CDN
VM operating-system disk
Lift-and-shift app needing NFS share

quiz.why: Amazon S3 is object storage, holding objects in buckets. EBS is block storage and EFS is file storage.
Azure Files provides managed SMB or NFS file shares.
Block storage gives low-latency volumes, so it is best for VM disks and databases. Archives and static websites use object storage.
Google's object storage is Cloud Storage. Filestore is file storage and Persistent Disk is block.

quiz.q: Default stance on bucket public access:
quiz.why: Block public bucket access unless truly needed, because public buckets are a common cause of data leaks.

lessons.title: Storage tiers, durability and redundancy

scenes.text: A company must keep invoices for years but rarely reads them.
Moving them to an archive tier cuts cost sharply.

steps.title: Access tiers
steps.body:
- **AWS S3:** Standard, Standard-IA (infrequent access), Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier classes (archive).
- **Azure Blob:** Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive.
- **Google Cloud Storage:** Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive.
Colder tiers = cheaper storage but higher retrieval cost/latency and minimum storage durations. Use **lifecycle rules** to move data automatically.

steps.title: Durability vs availability
steps.body: **Durability** = probability data isn't lost (S3 is designed for 99.999999999% — '11 nines' — durability). **Availability** = probability you can access it right now (lower, e.g. 99.9–99.99%).

steps.title: Azure redundancy options
steps.body:
- **LRS:** 3 copies in one data centre.
- **ZRS:** 3 copies across availability zones in a region.
- **GRS:** LRS + async copy to the paired secondary region (6 copies total).
- **GZRS:** ZRS + async copy to secondary region.
Read-access variants (RA-GRS, RA-GZRS) allow reads from the secondary.

steps.title: Solved example: lifecycle rule
steps.body: Logs: Hot for 30 days → Cool until 90 days → Archive until 7 years → delete. Saves cost while meeting retention rules.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Archiving data that's needed instantly (archive retrieval can take hours).
- Assuming LRS survives a zone failure — it doesn't.

activity.prompt: Match the Azure redundancy option.

quiz.why: Archive is the coldest Azure Blob tier, with the lowest storage price and slowest access.

quiz.q: S3 is designed for durability of:
quiz.why: S3 is designed for 99.999999999% durability, called 11 nines.

quiz.q: Survives a zone outage within a region:
quiz.why: ZRS (zone-redundant storage) keeps copies across zones, so data survives a zone outage within a region. LRS keeps copies in one data centre.
Lifecycle rules automatically move or delete data by age, which saves cost.
Google's coldest storage class is Archive. Glacier is AWS, and Cool is Azure.

sources: Amazon S3, Azure Storage, Google Cloud Storage documentation

scenes.text: A DBA spends nights patching and backing up a self-managed database on a VM.
A managed service does backups, patching and failover automatically.

steps.title: Services
steps.body:
- **AWS:** Amazon RDS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server) and **Aurora** (MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible).
- **Azure:** **Azure SQL Database** (PaaS), Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL.
- **Google Cloud:** **Cloud SQL** (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server), **AlloyDB** (PostgreSQL-compatible), **Spanner** (globally distributed relational).

steps.title: What 'managed' gives you
steps.body: Automated backups and point-in-time restore, patching, monitoring, **high availability** with a standby in another zone (e.g. RDS Multi-AZ, zone-redundant Azure SQL), **read replicas**, encryption options. You still own schema, queries, indexes, users and data.

steps.title: Solved example: choose
steps.body:
**a)** Lift-and-shift SQL Server app needing near-full compatibility on Azure → Azure SQL Managed Instance.
**b)** New PostgreSQL app on AWS needing HA → RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ or Aurora PostgreSQL.
**c)** Global inventory needing strong consistency across continents → Spanner.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating read replicas as backups.
- Publicly accessible database endpoints — keep them in private subnets.

activity.prompt: Match the managed database.

quiz.why: Managed databases typically automate backups, patching and failover. You still write queries, business logic and schemas.
Read replicas scale reads but are not backups, because they copy deletes and corruption too. They don't give point-in-time recovery.

quiz.q: Azure's near-full SQL Server compatibility PaaS:
quiz.why: Azure SQL Managed Instance offers near-full SQL Server compatibility as PaaS, suited to lift-and-shift migrations.
Database endpoints should usually be private to reduce exposure to the internet.
Spanner is Google's globally distributed relational database. Bigtable and Firestore are NoSQL.

scenes.text: A shopping app logs billions of clicks and needs fast lookups of carts.
Analysts also want dashboards across years of sales.

steps.title: NoSQL
steps.body:
- **AWS:** DynamoDB (key-value/document), ElastiCache (Redis/Memcached), DocumentDB.
- **Azure:** **Cosmos DB** (multi-model, global distribution, multiple consistency levels), Azure Cache for Redis.
- **Google Cloud:** Firestore (document), **Bigtable** (wide-column), Memorystore (Redis).

steps.title: Analytics / warehouses
steps.body:
- **AWS:** Redshift (warehouse), Athena (SQL on S3), Glue (ETL catalogue).
- **Azure:** Azure Synapse Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Data Factory (ETL).
- **Google Cloud:** **BigQuery** (serverless warehouse), Dataflow (stream/batch processing).

steps.title: Solved example: pick services
steps.body: Carts (fast key lookups) → DynamoDB / Cosmos DB / Firestore. Click stream analytics → BigQuery / Redshift / Synapse. Session cache → Redis service.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running big analytics queries on the production OLTP database.
- Choosing NoSQL without designing for access patterns (partition keys).

activity.prompt: Operational NoSQL or analytics warehouse?

items.text: DynamoDB
BigQuery
Cosmos DB
Redshift
Firestore
Azure Synapse Analytics

quiz.why: Cosmos DB is Azure's globally distributed multi-model database.
BigQuery is Google's serverless data warehouse.
DynamoDB is AWS's key-value and document database. Redshift is a warehouse and Athena queries data in S3.
Athena runs SQL directly on data stored in S3, querying it in place.
Heavy analytics belong in a data warehouse, not the production OLTP database, so they don't slow transactions.

questions.q: Azure's object storage:
questions.why: Azure's object storage is Blob Storage. Azure Files is for file shares and Managed Disks are block storage.

questions.q: VM boot disks use:
questions.why: VM boot disks use block storage, which provides low-latency volumes.

questions.q: BigQuery is:
questions.why: BigQuery is Google's data warehouse for analytics.

questions.q: Durability means:
questions.why: Durability means data is not lost over time. It is different from availability, which means being accessible now.

questions.q: Shared SMB drive on Azure:
questions.why: Azure Files provides shared SMB file shares. Blob is object storage and Disks are block.

questions.q: Coldest Google Cloud Storage class:
questions.why: Archive is the coldest Google Cloud Storage class, colder than Nearline and Coldline.

questions.q: GRS keeps how many copies?
questions.why: GRS keeps 6 copies: 3 in the primary region (LRS) and 3 in a secondary region.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Read replicas replace backups. Reason (R): Replicas copy deletes and corruption too.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: replicas copy deletes and corruption too, so they can't replace backups.

questions.q: AWS MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible cloud-native DB:
questions.why: Aurora is AWS's MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible cloud-native database.

questions.q: Survive a regional outage for blobs:
questions.why: GRS or GZRS copies blobs to a secondary region, so data survives a regional outage. LRS and ZRS stay within one region.

questions.q: Case: Compliance archive read once a year, 7-year retention. Best tier?
questions.why: For a rarely read archive kept for seven years, the Archive tier with lifecycle rules is the cheapest storage. Hot and Premium cost far more.

questions.q: Case: 50 Linux servers must share one NFS directory on AWS. Service?
questions.why: Amazon EFS provides a shared NFS file system that many Linux servers can mount. EBS attaches to one instance, and S3 Glacier and DynamoDB are different.

questions.q: Case: Analysts' queries slow the production DB. Best fix?
questions.why: Replicate data to a warehouse like Redshift, BigQuery or Synapse so analytics runs separately from the production DB. A bigger production VM only treats the symptom.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct across clouds?
questions.why: S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage are the object storage equivalents. The other sets mix unrelated services.

questions.q: Why can archive tiers be cheap yet costly to use?
options: Low storage price but high retrieval charges, delays and minimum durations
questions.why: Archive tiers have low storage prices but charge high retrieval fees, add delays and impose minimum storage durations. So they are cheap to keep but costly to use.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Cloud networking
courses.summary: Virtual networks and subnets with CIDR maths, security groups and firewalls, connecting to the internet and on-premises, and DNS/CDN services.
outcomes: Learners can size subnets with CIDR and reserved addresses
Learners can design public and private subnets
Learners can configure security groups/NSGs on least privilege
Learners can choose VPN vs dedicated connectivity and map DNS/CDN services

lessons.title: VPCs, VNets, subnets and CIDR

scenes.text: A team created a /28 subnet for a Kubernetes cluster. After a few nodes, no IPs were left.
A little CIDR maths up front would have saved a painful migration.

steps.title: Virtual networks
steps.body: **AWS VPC**, **Azure Virtual Network (VNet)**, **Google VPC network**. An isolated private network you define with an address range (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16), split into **subnets**. In AWS and Azure, subnets are tied to a zone/region scope differently: AWS subnets live in **one AZ**; Azure subnets span the region's zones; Google VPCs are **global** with **regional** subnets.

steps.title: CIDR maths
steps.body:
A /n block has **2^(32−n)** IPv4 addresses.
- /16 → 65,536 · /20 → 4,096 · /24 → 256 · /26 → 64 · /28 → 16
**Reserved:** AWS and Azure reserve **5** addresses per subnet; Google reserves **4** in a subnet's primary range. So an AWS/Azure /24 gives **251** usable.

steps.title: Solved example: plan subnets
steps.body:
VNet 10.0.0.0/16. Need: web (≈200 hosts), app (≈400), DB (≈50).
- web: /24 (256 − 5 = 251) ✔ → 10.0.0.0/24
- app: /23 (512 − 5 = 507) ✔ → 10.0.2.0/23
- DB: /26 (64 − 5 = 59) ✔ → 10.0.4.0/26
Leave room to grow; avoid overlapping ranges with on-prem networks.

steps.title: Public vs private subnets
steps.body: **Public** subnet: route to the internet gateway (load balancers, bastions). **Private** subnet: no direct inbound internet route (app servers, databases); outbound via NAT.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Overlapping CIDRs with on-prem or other VNets → peering/VPN impossible.
- Tiny subnets for autoscaling or Kubernetes.
- Databases in public subnets.

activity.prompt: Read a CIDR prefix length n (e.g. 24) and a reserved count r. Print usable addresses = 2**(32-n) - r.
activity.starter:
n, r = map(int, input().split())
# compute usable addresses
activity.solution:
n, r = map(int, input().split())
print(2 ** (32 - n) - r)

quiz.why: A /26 has 32 − 26 = 6 host bits, so 2⁶ = 64 addresses.

quiz.q: Usable IPs in an AWS /24 subnet:
quiz.why: AWS reserves 5 addresses in each subnet, so a /24 has 256 − 5 = 251 usable IPs.
An AWS subnet lives in exactly one availability zone. A VPC spans the region.
Databases normally go in private subnets, so they have no inbound internet route.
Overlapping CIDR ranges cause routing conflicts, which block peering and VPN connectivity.

sources: AWS VPC, Azure VNet, Google VPC documentation

scenes.text: A developer opens SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0 'just for today'.
Within hours, bots are trying passwords on it.

steps.title: Instance-level rules
steps.body:
- **AWS security groups:** stateful allow-rules attached to instances/ENIs; return traffic automatically allowed.
- **AWS network ACLs:** stateless allow/deny rules at subnet level.
- **Azure network security groups (NSGs):** stateful allow/deny rules with priorities, on subnets or NICs.
- **Google VPC firewall rules / policies:** stateful rules applied by network tags or service accounts.

steps.title: Managed firewalls and WAF
steps.body: Centralised firewalls (AWS Network Firewall, Azure Firewall, Cloud NGFW) inspect traffic across networks. A **web application firewall (WAF)** on an L7 load balancer/CDN blocks common web attacks (e.g. SQL injection).

steps.title: Solved example: three-tier rules
steps.body:
- **Web SG:** allow 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (via load balancer).
- **App SG:** allow 8080 **only from Web SG**.
- **DB SG:** allow 5432 **only from App SG**.
- **Admin:** no public SSH/RDP — use a bastion service (AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, Azure Bastion, Google IAP TCP forwarding).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH (22) or RDP (3389).
- Allowing all ports between tiers.
- Forgetting NACLs are stateless (need rules for return traffic).

statements.s: AWS security groups are stateful.
AWS network ACLs are stateful.
Opening RDP 3389 to 0.0.0.0/0 is good practice.
Azure NSG rules are processed by priority number (lower first).
Referencing another security group as a source is a least-privilege technique.

quiz.why: Azure's network filtering rule set is the network security group (NSG). Security groups and VPC firewalls are AWS and Google terms.
Network ACLs are AWS's stateless subnet-level rules. Security groups are stateful and attach to instances.

quiz.q: Safe admin access without public SSH:
quiz.why: Use a bastion or session manager service for admin access, so you don't expose port 22 publicly. Opening SSH to all or emailing keys is unsafe.

options: Common web attacks like SQL injection
quiz.why: A web application firewall (WAF) blocks common web attacks like SQL injection at layer 7. It doesn't deal with disk failure or billing.

quiz.q: DB tier should accept traffic only from:
quiz.why: The DB tier should accept traffic only from the app tier, following least privilege. Opening it to the internet or all networks adds risk.

lessons.title: Internet, NAT, peering and hybrid connectivity

scenes.text: A manufacturer wants its factory network to reach cloud apps privately and reliably.
It starts with a VPN, then moves to a dedicated connection as traffic grows.

steps.title: Internet access
steps.body:
- **Internet gateway** (AWS) / default internet routing (Azure, Google) for public subnets.
- **NAT gateway** lets private instances make **outbound** connections (updates, APIs) without accepting inbound connections. AWS NAT Gateway, Azure NAT Gateway, Google Cloud NAT.

steps.title: Connecting networks
steps.body:
- **Peering:** connect two VPCs/VNets privately (VPC peering, VNet peering, VPC Network Peering). Not transitive by default.
- **Hubs:** AWS Transit Gateway, Azure Virtual WAN / hub-spoke, Google Network Connectivity Center.
- **Site-to-site VPN:** encrypted tunnel over the internet — quick, cheaper, variable performance.
- **Dedicated private links:** **AWS Direct Connect**, **Azure ExpressRoute**, **Google Cloud Interconnect** — private, consistent bandwidth and latency.

steps.title: Solved example: choose connectivity
steps.body:
**a)** Pilot with 50 Mbps needs, go live next week → site-to-site VPN.
**b)** Bank moving core systems, needs predictable latency and high bandwidth → ExpressRoute/Direct Connect/Interconnect (often with VPN as backup).
**c)** Private VMs need OS updates → NAT gateway.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting peering A↔B and B↔C to give A↔C — use a hub.
- Giving private servers public IPs just for updates — use NAT.

activity.prompt: Match the need to the service.
pairs: Private servers need outbound internet only
Hub to connect many VPCs in AWS

quiz.why: A NAT gateway allows outbound-only internet access from private subnets. It doesn't allow inbound connections.
ExpressRoute is Azure's dedicated private connection. Direct Connect is AWS and Cloud Interconnect is Google.
Peering is non-transitive by default, so A cannot reach C through B unless it is peered with C.

quiz.q: Quickest to set up hybrid link:
quiz.why: A site-to-site VPN is the quickest hybrid link to set up, since it runs over the internet. Dedicated lines take time to provision.
Google's dedicated private connection is Cloud Interconnect. Direct Connect is AWS and ExpressRoute is Azure.

scenes.text: A school moves its website to the cloud and wants users routed to the healthy, nearest copy.
Cloud DNS with health checks plus a CDN does it.

steps.title: DNS services
steps.body: **Amazon Route 53**, **Azure DNS** (plus **Traffic Manager** for DNS-based routing), **Google Cloud DNS**. Routing policies include simple, weighted, latency-based, geolocation and failover with health checks (Route 53 and Traffic Manager).

steps.title: CDN services
steps.body: **Amazon CloudFront**, **Azure Front Door / Azure CDN**, **Google Cloud CDN**. Cache static and media content at edge locations; integrate with WAF and TLS certificates.

steps.title: Solved example: failover
steps.body: Primary site in Mumbai region, standby in Hyderabad region. DNS failover policy with health checks: if Mumbai fails health checks, DNS answers point to Hyderabad. Keep TTLs low (e.g. 60 s) so clients switch quickly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Very long DNS TTLs before a migration.
- Caching personalised pages at the CDN.

activity.prompt: Match the service.

quiz.why: Low DNS TTLs make clients re-query sooner, so failover and migration take effect faster.
CloudFront is AWS's CDN. Route 53 is DNS and S3 is storage.
Traffic Manager is Azure's DNS-based traffic routing service. ExpressRoute and Bastion do other jobs.
Latency-based routing sends users to the endpoint with the lowest latency, which improves performance.
Cloud DNS is Google's DNS service. Route 53 is AWS and Azure DNS is Azure.

questions.q: Azure's private network:
questions.why: Azure's private network is the Virtual Network (VNet). VPC is the AWS and Google term.

questions.q: Addresses in /24:
questions.why: A /24 has 8 host bits, so 2⁸ = 256 addresses.

questions.q: AWS DNS service:
questions.why: Route 53 is AWS's DNS service. Direct Connect and CloudFront do other jobs.

questions.q: Private subnets reach the internet outbound via:
questions.why: A NAT gateway lets private subnets reach the internet outbound without exposing them to inbound connections.

questions.q: Stateful AWS instance firewall:
questions.why: A security group is AWS's stateful instance-level firewall. A NACL is stateless and works at the subnet level.

questions.q: Dedicated private link to AWS:
questions.why: Direct Connect is the dedicated private link to AWS. ExpressRoute is Azure and Interconnect is Google.

questions.q: Usable IPs in an Azure /27 subnet:
questions.why: Azure reserves 5 addresses per subnet, so a /27 (32 addresses) has 32 − 5 = 27 usable.

questions.q: Assertion (A): VPC peering A–B and B–C lets A reach C. Reason (R): Peering is non-transitive.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: peering is non-transitive, so A–B and B–C peering doesn't let A reach C.

questions.q: Google VPC networks are:
questions.why: Google VPC networks are global, with regional subnets. They are not zonal or per VM.

questions.q: NACLs require explicit rules for return traffic because they are:
questions.why: NACLs are stateless, so they need explicit rules for return traffic. Stateful firewalls allow replies automatically.

questions.q: Case: Need 450 usable IPs in one AWS subnet. Smallest prefix?
questions.why: A /24 has 251 usable IPs in AWS, which is too few, and a /23 has 512 − 5 = 507. So /23 is the smallest prefix that gives 450 usable IPs.

questions.q: Case: Admins need SSH to private Linux VMs on Azure without public IPs. Service?
questions.why: Azure Bastion gives SSH or RDP access to private VMs without public IPs. DNS, Blob and Front Door don't do that.

questions.q: Case: Bank needs consistent low-latency private connectivity to Azure with backup. Design?
questions.why: ExpressRoute as the primary gives consistent low-latency private connectivity, and a site-to-site VPN as backup adds resilience. Public internet or VPN only is less reliable.

questions.q: Case: DB SG allows 0.0.0.0/0 on 5432. Best correction?
options: Allow 5432 only from the app tier's SG
questions.why: Allowing 5432 only from the app tier's security group follows least privilege. Opening it to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the database to the whole internet.

questions.q: Case: 30 VPCs must interconnect plus on-prem. Simplest scalable design on AWS?
questions.why: A Transit Gateway hub connects many VPCs and on-prem simply and scalably. Full-mesh peering of 30 VPCs would need 435 links and is non-transitive.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Identity, security and governance
courses.summary: IAM models on each cloud, resource hierarchies, least privilege and protecting the most powerful accounts, encryption and key management, and governance with policies, tags, locks and audit logs.
outcomes: Learners can explain AWS IAM, Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC, and Google Cloud IAM
Learners can describe each cloud's resource hierarchy
Learners can secure root/global admin accounts and use roles instead of keys
Learners can use KMS/Key Vault/Cloud KMS and secrets managers
Learners can apply governance with policies, tags, locks and audit logs

lessons.title: IAM models and resource hierarchies

scenes.text: An auditor asks a simple question: 'Who can delete your production database?'
The cloud team realises they need to understand identities, roles and scopes properly.

steps.title: AWS
steps.body: **IAM** users, groups, **roles** (assumed temporarily by people, services or other accounts) and **policies** (JSON documents allowing/denying actions on resources). **AWS IAM Identity Center** gives workforce single sign-on. **AWS Organizations** groups accounts into organisational units (OUs).

steps.title: Azure
steps.body: **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD) holds identities (users, groups, service principals, managed identities). **Azure RBAC** assigns roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader, and many specific roles) at a **scope**: management group → subscription → resource group → resource. Permissions are **inherited** downward.

steps.title: Google Cloud
steps.body: **Cloud IAM** grants **roles** (basic, predefined, custom) to **principals** (Google accounts, groups, service accounts) on resources in the hierarchy: **organisation → folders → projects → resources**. Policies are inherited downward.

steps.title: Solved example: effective access in Azure
steps.body:
Riya has **Reader** at subscription scope and **Contributor** on resource group 'rg-web'.
- In 'rg-web' she can create/modify resources (Contributor; RBAC is additive).
- Elsewhere in the subscription she can only read.
- She **cannot** assign roles (needs Owner or User Access Administrator).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Granting Owner at subscription level 'to save time'.
- Using basic roles (Owner/Editor) in Google Cloud where predefined roles fit.
- Long-lived access keys in code.

activity.prompt: Order the Azure scope hierarchy from broadest to narrowest.

quiz.why: Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure AD, is Azure's identity service. AWS IAM is AWS's.
Google Cloud's hierarchy runs organisation, folders, projects, then resources. Subscriptions and resource groups are Azure terms.

options: An identity assumed temporarily with permissions
quiz.why: An AWS role is an identity that is assumed temporarily and carries permissions, with temporary credentials.

options: Manage resources but not assign roles
quiz.why: Azure Contributor can manage resources but cannot assign roles. Owner can.

quiz.q: Permissions assigned at a parent scope are:
quiz.why: Permissions assigned at a parent scope are inherited by the child scopes beneath it.

sources: AWS IAM, Microsoft Entra & Azure RBAC, Google Cloud IAM documentation

lessons.title: Least privilege and protecting powerful accounts

scenes.text: A developer commits an access key to a public repository.
Within minutes, bots launch crypto-mining VMs on the account.

steps.title: Protect the top accounts
steps.body:
- **AWS root user:** enable MFA, don't create access keys for it, use only for the few tasks that require it.
- **Azure Global Administrator / subscription Owners:** few people, phishing-resistant MFA, **Privileged Identity Management (PIM)** for just-in-time elevation.
- **Google Cloud organisation admins:** few, MFA, use groups.

steps.title: Roles and managed identities instead of keys
steps.body: Workloads should use **temporary credentials**: IAM roles for EC2/Lambda, **managed identities** in Azure, **service accounts** attached to Google resources (avoid downloading service-account keys). No secrets in code.

steps.title: Solved example: least-privilege policy
steps.body:
An app only needs to read objects from one bucket.
**Too broad:** `s3:*` on `*`.
**Right:** allow `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*` only, attached to the app's role.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shared admin accounts.
- Never reviewing unused permissions (use access analysers/recommenders).
- Secrets in environment files committed to Git.

activity.prompt: Cloud identity hardening checklist
items: No access keys for the AWS root user

quiz.q: Best credential for an app on an Azure VM:
quiz.why: A managed identity gives an app on an Azure VM a credential without any secret to store or leak. Passwords in code or shared accounts are risky.

options: Have MFA and no access keys
quiz.why: The AWS root user should have MFA and no access keys, and not be used daily. It has unlimited power, so protect it.
Azure PIM (Privileged Identity Management) provides just-in-time privileged access, elevating roles on demand.
s3:* on * grants every S3 action on every resource, which violates least privilege. Permissions should be scoped narrowly.

quiz.q: Leaked keys in public repos are typically abused:
quiz.why: Leaked keys in public repos are typically abused within minutes, because attackers run automated scanners.

scenes.text: A hospital's compliance team asks: is patient data encrypted, and who controls the keys?
The cloud architect explains provider-managed vs customer-managed keys.

steps.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
steps.body: **At rest:** storage and databases encrypt data on disk (often on by default). **In transit:** TLS for connections. Options: **provider-managed keys** (simplest) or **customer-managed keys (CMK)** for more control, rotation and revocation.

steps.title: Key and secret services
steps.body:
- **AWS KMS** (keys), **AWS Secrets Manager** / Parameter Store (secrets)
- **Azure Key Vault** (keys, secrets, certificates)
- **Google Cloud KMS**, **Secret Manager**

steps.title: Solved example: database password
steps.body:
**Wrong:** password in `config.yaml` in Git.
**Right:** store in Key Vault / Secrets Manager / Secret Manager; app reads it at runtime using its managed identity/role; enable rotation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deleting a customer-managed key → data encrypted with it becomes unrecoverable (use deletion protection/soft delete).
- Disabling TLS for 'internal' traffic.

activity.prompt: Match the service to its job.
pairs: Keys, secrets and certificates on Azure
Store and rotate secrets on AWS

quiz.why: Encryption in transit uses TLS. RBAC, CIDR and LRS are unrelated to it.
Customer-managed keys give more control over key rotation and revocation than provider-managed keys.
Database passwords belong in a secrets manager or vault, where access is central and audited. Wikis, email and source code leak.
Deleting a customer-managed key can make the encrypted data unrecoverable, a form of crypto-shredding.
Azure's key and secret service is Key Vault.

lessons.title: Governance: policies, tags, locks and audit logs

story.title: The VM in the wrong country

scenes.text: A team spins up resources in a region outside India, breaking a data-residency rule.
A policy that only allows Indian regions prevents it from happening again.

steps.title: Policy guardrails
steps.body:
- **AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs):** set the maximum permissions for accounts in an OU (e.g. deny non-approved regions).
- **Azure Policy:** evaluate and enforce rules on resources (allowed locations, required tags, allowed VM sizes); initiatives group policies.
- **Google Cloud Organization Policy Service:** constraints like allowed resource locations.

steps.title: Tags and locks
steps.body: **Tags/labels** (e.g. `owner=finance`, `env=prod`, `costcentre=CC42`) support cost reports and automation. **Azure resource locks:** **CanNotDelete** (delete blocked) and **ReadOnly** (changes blocked) — even for Owners until removed.

steps.title: Audit logs and posture
steps.body: Who did what, when: **AWS CloudTrail**, **Azure Activity Log** (with Azure Monitor), **Google Cloud Audit Logs**. Security posture tools: AWS Security Hub/GuardDuty, **Microsoft Defender for Cloud**, Google **Security Command Center**.

steps.title: Solved example: guardrails for a regulated team
steps.body: 1) Policy: allowed locations = Indian regions only. 2) Policy: require tags owner, env, costcentre. 3) Lock: CanNotDelete on production database. 4) Send audit logs to a central, immutable log account/workspace. 5) Enable posture management alerts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Relying on 'please don't' emails instead of enforced policy.
- Logs stored only in the same account an attacker could control.

activity.prompt: Match the tool to its purpose.
pairs: Cap permissions for AWS accounts in an OU
Block deletion of an Azure resource
Azure security posture and threat protection

quiz.q: To restrict Azure resources to Indian regions use:
quiz.why: Azure Policy with the allowed-locations rule enforces that resources are created only in chosen regions, such as Indian ones. Tags and DNS don't enforce this.
A ReadOnly lock prevents changes and deletions to a resource. A CanNotDelete lock only blocks deletion.
AWS CloudTrail records API activity for audit. Route 53 and CloudFront do other jobs.
Tags are metadata that help with cost allocation and automation. They don't encrypt or route.
SCPs (service control policies) set the maximum available permissions as guardrails. They don't grant permissions themselves.

sources: Azure Policy, AWS Organizations, Google Organization Policy documentation

questions.q: Azure RBAC role that can assign roles:
questions.why: Owner can assign roles in Azure RBAC, as can User Access Administrator. Contributor, Reader and Viewer cannot.

questions.q: Google Cloud resources are grouped in:
questions.why: Google Cloud resources are grouped in projects. Resource groups are an Azure concept.

questions.q: Audit log on Azure:
questions.why: Azure's audit log of control-plane activity is the Activity Log. CloudTrail is AWS and Audit Logs is Google.

questions.q: Best credential for workloads:
questions.why: Roles and managed identities give workloads temporary credentials, which are safer than root keys or long-lived keys.

questions.q: Key Vault stores:
questions.why: Key Vault stores keys, secrets and certificates, not VMs, DNS or logs.

questions.q: Azure scope order:
options: Management group > subscription > resource group > resource
questions.why: Azure scope runs management group, subscription, resource group, then resource, from broadest to narrowest.

questions.q: Assertion (A): An SCP alone can grant an IAM user access. Reason (R): SCPs set the maximum permissions available.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: an SCP only sets the maximum permissions and cannot grant access by itself.

questions.q: Reader at subscription + Contributor on RG-A: in RG-A the user can:
questions.why: Azure RBAC is additive, so in RG-A the user's Contributor role lets them modify resources, even though Reader at subscription level only reads.

questions.q: Customer-managed keys mainly add:
questions.why: Customer-managed keys mainly add control over the key lifecycle, such as rotation and revocation. They don't speed things up or make anything public.

questions.q: Lock that blocks deletion but allows changes:
questions.why: A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion but still allows changes. ReadOnly blocks both.

questions.q: Case: Access key found in a public repo. First actions?
options: Deactivate/rotate key, review CloudTrail, remove from repo history
questions.why: Deactivate or rotate the exposed key, review CloudTrail for misuse and remove it from repo history. Deleting the repo alone leaves the key valid.

questions.q: Case: Teams keep creating untagged resources, breaking cost reports. Fix?
questions.why: An Azure Policy or organisation policy that requires tags enforces the rule, rather than hoping teams comply.

questions.q: Case: Google Cloud app uses a downloaded service-account key file. Better?
options: Attach the service account to the resource (no key file)
questions.why: Attach the service account to the resource so no key file exists. Downloaded key files are long-lived secrets that can leak.

questions.q: Which is the most complete least-privilege fix for an app needing read access to one bucket?
options: Role with GetObject on that bucket's objects only
questions.why: A role allowing only GetObject on that bucket's objects follows least privilege with scoped action and resource. AdministratorAccess, s3:* on * and root are far too broad.

questions.q: Why send audit logs to a separate, locked account/workspace?
options: An attacker in the workload account can't erase the evidence
questions.why: Sending audit logs to a separate, locked account means an attacker in the workload account can't erase the evidence. This gives tamper resistance.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Cost management and well-architected design
courses.summary: Pricing factors and cost tools, practical cost optimisation, the Well-Architected Framework pillars, and reliability with SLAs, RTO/RPO and disaster-recovery strategies.
outcomes: Learners can list factors that affect cloud cost and use budgets and alerts
Learners can apply six cost-optimisation levers
Learners can name the AWS and Azure Well-Architected pillars
Learners can compute composite SLAs and choose a DR strategy from RTO/RPO

lessons.title: Pricing factors and cost tools

scenes.text: A student project's bill jumps to ₹45,000 because a GPU VM was left running for a month.
A budget alert at ₹2,000 would have caught it in a day.

steps.title: What drives cost
steps.body: Resource type and size, **running time**, region, storage amount and tier, **data transfer out** (egress to the internet/other regions is usually charged; ingress usually free), requests/operations, licences, support plan, and commitment discounts.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body:
- Estimating: **AWS Pricing Calculator**, **Azure Pricing Calculator**, **Google Cloud Pricing Calculator**; Azure TCO calculator to compare with on-prem.
- Tracking: **AWS Cost Explorer & Budgets**, **Microsoft Cost Management (with budgets)**, **Google Cloud Billing reports & budgets**.
- Use tags/labels for cost allocation.

steps.title: Solved example: monthly estimate
steps.body:
2 VMs × ₹6/hour × 730 h = ₹8,760
500 GB storage × ₹1.8/GB = ₹900
200 GB egress × ₹7/GB = ₹1,400
**Total ≈ ₹11,060/month** (illustrative prices). Biggest lever: VM hours.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring egress charges for media-heavy apps.
- No budgets or alerts.
- Orphaned disks, snapshots and public IPs after deleting VMs.

activity.prompt: 3 VMs at ₹5/hour run 730 hours each in a month. VM cost in ₹?

quiz.why: Data transfer out to the internet (egress) is usually charged. Inbound transfer is usually free.

quiz.q: Tool to compare on-prem vs Azure:
quiz.why: The TCO calculator compares the total cost of ownership of on-premises with Azure.
Budget alerts notify you early when spending nears a limit, so you can catch overspending.
A month has about 730 hours, as 8,760 hours a year ÷ 12 ≈ 730.
Orphaned resources, like unattached disks and snapshots, still cost money while delivering no value.

sources: Provider pricing and cost management documentation

scenes.text: A FinOps review at an ed-tech firm finds idle dev environments, oversized VMs and hot-tier archives.
Three months later, the bill is 40% lower with no loss of performance.

steps.title: Six levers
steps.body:
1) **Right-size** to actual utilisation.
2) **Turn off** non-production at night/weekends (schedules).
3) **Commit** for steady load (reservations, savings plans, committed use).
4) **Spot** for interruptible work.
5) **Tier storage** with lifecycle rules; delete orphans.
6) **Architect** for cost: serverless/autoscale, CDN to cut egress, managed services to cut ops effort.

steps.title: Solved example: dev environment schedule
steps.body:
Dev VMs needed 10 h × 5 days = 50 h/week instead of 168 h.
Saving = 1 − 50/168 ≈ **70%** of dev compute cost.

steps.title: FinOps culture
steps.body: Make cost visible to teams (showback/chargeback by tags), set budgets per team, review monthly, and treat cost as an engineering metric like latency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Buying 3-year reservations before right-sizing.
- Optimising tiny line items while ignoring the top three costs.

activity.label: Hours per week your dev environment runs

bands.text: Great — scheduled for working hours; roughly 70% or more saved versus 24×7.
Some savings; consider stricter schedules or auto-shutdown when idle.
Running nearly 24×7 — schedule shutdowns for nights and weekends.

quiz.why: Right-size first, so you don't commit to oversized capacity. Reservations on the wrong size lock in waste.
Running 50 of 168 weekly hours saves 1 − 50/168 ≈ 70%.
A CDN serves content from the edge, which reduces egress from the origin.

options: Cost visibility and accountability by team
quiz.why: FinOps emphasises cost visibility and accountability by team. It is a shared culture, not only finance control.
Spot suits interruptible work because it can be reclaimed. Databases, payment APIs and domain controllers need to stay up.

scenes.text: Before launch, a team runs a well-architected review.
It finds a single-AZ database (reliability) and no budget alerts (cost).

steps.title: AWS Well-Architected (6 pillars)
steps.body: **Operational excellence**, **Security**, **Reliability**, **Performance efficiency**, **Cost optimization**, **Sustainability**.

steps.title: Azure Well-Architected Framework (5 pillars)
steps.body: **Reliability**, **Security**, **Cost optimization**, **Operational excellence**, **Performance efficiency**. Google Cloud publishes a similar Architecture Framework.

steps.title: Solved example: map findings to pillars
steps.body:
- No MFA on admin → **Security**
- Single-AZ DB → **Reliability**
- Manual deployments with no runbooks → **Operational excellence**
- Oversized VMs → **Cost optimization** (and Sustainability)
- No caching for a read-heavy API → **Performance efficiency**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating pillars separately — they trade off (e.g. multi-region raises reliability and cost).
- Reviewing only once, never after changes.

activity.prompt: Which pillar does each finding belong to?

items.text: Database not replicated across zones
Access keys in source code
Idle VMs running all weekend
No automated deployment pipeline
No backups tested
No budget alerts

quiz.q: AWS Well-Architected has how many pillars?
quiz.why: AWS Well-Architected has six pillars, including sustainability.

quiz.q: Azure WAF has how many pillars?
quiz.why: The Azure Well-Architected Framework has five pillars.

quiz.q: Single-AZ database is a gap in:
quiz.why: A single-AZ database is a gap in reliability, since an AZ failure would take it down. It is a fault-tolerance issue.
Sustainability is the sixth pillar in the AWS Well-Architected Framework. Azure's five pillars don't include it.
Manual, undocumented deployments hurt operational excellence, which covers automation and repeatable operations.

scenes.text: The CFO asks: 'If the region fails, how long are we down, and how much data do we lose?'
Those are RTO and RPO — and they decide the DR design and cost.

steps.title: SLAs
steps.body: A provider **SLA** states promised uptime (e.g. 99.9%, 99.95%, 99.99%) and service credits if missed — usually only for supported configurations (e.g. multiple instances across zones). **Composite SLA** for dependent services = **product** of SLAs: App 99.95% × DB 99.99% ≈ **99.94%**.

steps.title: RTO and RPO
steps.body:
- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** maximum acceptable downtime.
- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time (e.g. last 15 minutes of data).

steps.title: DR strategies (cheapest → fastest)
steps.body:
1) **Backup & restore:** hours–days RTO; cheapest.
2) **Pilot light:** core data replicated, minimal services ready; scale up on disaster.
3) **Warm standby:** scaled-down full copy running.
4) **Multi-site active-active:** full capacity in two+ regions; near-zero RTO/RPO; most expensive.

steps.title: Solved example: choose a strategy
steps.body:
Requirement: RTO 1 hour, RPO 5 minutes, moderate budget.
- Backup & restore (RTO hours, RPO 24 h) ✘
- Pilot light with continuous DB replication → RPO minutes, RTO ~1 h ✔ (or warm standby if scale-up is slow).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Never testing failover.
- Assuming the provider SLA covers your single-instance design.
- Confusing RTO (time down) with RPO (data lost).

activity.prompt: Composite SLA (in %) for a web app at 99.95% depending on a database at 99.99%? (two decimals)

quiz.why: RPO (recovery point objective) measures acceptable data loss. RTO measures acceptable downtime.
Backup and restore is the cheapest DR strategy because it needs the least standing infrastructure, but it has the slowest recovery.

quiz.q: Composite SLA of dependent services is the:
quiz.why: For dependent services in series, the composite SLA is the product of the individual SLAs. It is lower than any single one.
Near-zero RTO and RPO need multi-site active-active, with full redundancy in more than one location.

options: Service must be restored within 4 hours
quiz.why: An RTO of 4 hours means the service must be restored within 4 hours of an outage. It is not about data loss or backup frequency.

questions.q: Data transfer typically charged:
questions.why: Data transfer out (egress) is typically charged, while inbound is usually free.

questions.q: RTO is:
questions.why: RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime. RPO is the maximum data loss.

questions.q: AWS cost analysis tool:
questions.why: AWS Cost Explorer is the tool to analyse AWS costs. IAM, Route 53 and CloudTrail do other jobs.

questions.q: Pillar common to AWS and Azure frameworks:
questions.why: Reliability is a pillar in both the AWS and Azure frameworks. Sustainability is only an AWS pillar.

questions.q: Most expensive DR strategy:
questions.why: Active-active multi-site is the most expensive DR strategy because it duplicates the full environment.

questions.q: Right-sizing addresses:
questions.why: Right-sizing addresses oversized resources, so you stop paying for capacity you don't use.

questions.q: Composite SLA 99.9% × 99.9% ≈
questions.why: Composite SLA is the product: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, which is 99.8%.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Provider SLAs apply to any design. Reason (R): Many SLAs require redundant deployments such as multiple instances across zones.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: many SLAs only apply if you deploy redundantly, such as multiple instances across zones.

questions.q: Sustainability is a pillar of:
questions.why: Sustainability is a pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework, as its sixth. Azure's five pillars don't list it.

questions.q: Case: RTO 15 min, RPO near zero for payments. Strategy?
options: Active-active or hot standby with synchronous/near-sync replication
questions.why: RTO 15 minutes and near-zero RPO need active-active or hot standby with synchronous or near-synchronous replication. Daily backups or pilot light recover far too slowly.

questions.q: Case: Dev environments run 168 h/week but are used 60 h. Saving by scheduling?
questions.why: Used 60 of 168 hours, so scheduling saves 1 − 60/168 ≈ 64%.

questions.q: Case: Bill is dominated by internet egress from a video app. Best lever?
questions.why: When internet egress dominates the bill, CDN caching and compression cut the data leaving the origin. More regions or bigger VMs don't reduce egress.

questions.q: Composite: LB 99.99% → App 99.95% → DB 99.99% ≈
questions.why: Composite availability is the product: 0.9999 × 0.9995 × 0.9999 ≈ 0.9993, which is 99.93%.

questions.q: Why right-size before buying reservations?
options: Otherwise you lock in paying for unused capacity for 1–3 years
questions.why: Right-size first, otherwise you lock in paying for unused capacity for one to three years. Reservations are commitments, so the size must be right.

courses.title: Cloud · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: A cross-cloud service map and formula sheet, a scenario drill, and a full mock test. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any exam provider.
outcomes: Learners can map equivalent services across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
Learners can solve cloud numericals (CIDR, SLA, cost)
Learners can score 80%+ on the mock

scenes.text: Arjun is preparing for AZ-900 but his team uses AWS too.
He builds one table mapping equivalent services.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body:
VMs: EC2 · Azure Virtual Machines · Compute Engine
Autoscaling: Auto Scaling groups · VM Scale Sets · Managed instance groups
Kubernetes: EKS · AKS · GKE
Functions: Lambda · Azure Functions · Cloud Run functions

steps.title: Storage & data
steps.body:
Object: S3 · Blob Storage · Cloud Storage
Block: EBS · Managed Disks · Persistent Disk
File: EFS · Azure Files · Filestore
Relational: RDS/Aurora · Azure SQL Database · Cloud SQL/Spanner
NoSQL: DynamoDB · Cosmos DB · Firestore/Bigtable
Warehouse: Redshift · Synapse/Fabric · BigQuery

steps.title: Network & security
steps.body:
Network: VPC · VNet · VPC network
Private link: Direct Connect · ExpressRoute · Cloud Interconnect
DNS: Route 53 · Azure DNS · Cloud DNS
CDN: CloudFront · Front Door/CDN · Cloud CDN
Identity: IAM/Identity Center · Entra ID + RBAC · Cloud IAM
Keys: KMS · Key Vault · Cloud KMS
Audit: CloudTrail · Activity Log · Cloud Audit Logs
Guardrails: SCPs · Azure Policy · Organization Policy

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Addresses = 2^(32−prefix); usable AWS/Azure = − 5; Google = − 4
- Composite SLA = product
- Monthly hours ≈ 730
- GB-seconds = invocations × seconds × GB

activity.prompt: Match the AWS service to its Azure equivalent.

quiz.why: Cosmos DB is Azure's NoSQL database, the equivalent of AWS DynamoDB.
Google's equivalent of AWS EBS block storage is Persistent Disk.
Azure Policy is Azure's equivalent of guardrails like AWS SCPs, as it enforces rules on resources.

quiz.q: Usable IPs in a Google /24 primary range:
quiz.why: Google reserves 4 addresses in a primary subnet range, so a /24 has 256 − 4 = 252 usable IPs.

scenes.text: The lead architect fires quick scenarios at the team.
Answer each in one line.

steps.title: Drill 1
steps.body: Private VMs need patches from the internet → **NAT gateway**.

steps.title: Drill 2
steps.body: Keep data in India only → **policy for allowed regions** + choose Indian regions.

steps.title: Drill 3
steps.body: App needs DB password → **secrets manager/Key Vault + managed identity/role**.

steps.title: Drill 4
steps.body: Logs read rarely, retained 7 years → **archive tier + lifecycle rule**.

steps.title: Drill 5
steps.body: Survive one data-centre failure → **deploy across ≥2–3 AZs behind a load balancer**.

steps.title: Drill 6
steps.body: Interruptible nightly batch → **spot capacity**.

activity.prompt: Pick the right category of answer.

items.text: Use a NAT gateway
Use managed identity instead of keys
Buy savings plan for steady load
Deploy across three availability zones
Enable MFA on root
Schedule dev VMs off at night

quiz.why: Multi-AZ deployment survives the failure of a data centre. A bigger VM or archive tier doesn't.
Spot is the cheapest option for interruptible batch work, offering large discounts for capacity that may be reclaimed.
Keep secrets out of code by using a vault plus a managed identity. Wikis, email and Git files leak.
A policy or guardrail enforces India-only regions. Tags, DNS and CDN don't enforce locations.

scenes.text: Take the mock under time, then review every explanation.
Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.

steps.title: Elimination
steps.body: Remove answers from the wrong cloud first (e.g. 'ExpressRoute' in an AWS question), then wrong category (storage vs compute), then pick the most managed/least-privilege option.

steps.title: Disclaimer
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.

steps.title: Hands-on
