steps.body: Use free tiers/sandboxes to create a VNet/VPC, a VM, a bucket and a budget alert — then delete everything.

activity.prompt: Which cloud service family do you still mix up across providers? Write the three names side by side.
activity.hint: e.g. 'Object storage: S3 / Blob / Cloud Storage'.

options: Remove answers from the wrong cloud
quiz.why: Remove answers from the wrong cloud first, as the exam context tells you which provider's services apply. It narrows the choices.
Delete resources after hands-on labs to avoid charges. Leaving them running or sharing keys costs money or causes risk.

quiz.q: Exam guides should be checked because:
quiz.why: Check exam guides because skills outlines change. Relying on old versions may miss new topics.

questions.q: IaaS example:
questions.why: Azure Virtual Machines is IaaS, as you manage the OS. Microsoft 365 and Gmail are SaaS, and App Service is PaaS.

questions.q: Object storage on AWS:
questions.why: S3 is AWS's object storage. EBS is block, EFS is file and RDS is a database service.

questions.q: Azure identity:
questions.why: Entra ID is Azure's identity service. IAM is AWS and Cloud IAM is Google.

questions.q: Elasticity means:
questions.why: Elasticity means automatic scale out and in with demand. Fixed capacity or manual tickets are the opposite.

questions.q: Google warehouse:
questions.why: BigQuery is Google's data warehouse. Cloud SQL, Firestore and Bigtable serve other needs.

questions.q: Shared SMB share on Azure:
questions.why: Azure Files provides shared SMB file shares. Blob is object storage and Managed Disk is block.

questions.q: Outbound-only internet for private subnet:
questions.why: A NAT gateway gives a private subnet outbound-only internet access.

questions.q: Customer always responsible for:
questions.why: Data and identities are always the customer's responsibility under shared responsibility. The provider handles the hypervisor, physical security and data-centre power.

questions.q: Usable IPs in an AWS /25:
questions.why: A /25 has 128 addresses and AWS reserves 5 in each subnet, so 128 − 5 = 123 usable.

questions.q: Assertion (A): ZRS survives a zone failure. Reason (R): ZRS keeps copies across availability zones.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: ZRS keeps copies across availability zones, so storage survives a single-zone failure.

questions.q: Composite SLA 99.95% × 99.9% ≈
questions.why: Composite SLA is the product: 0.9995 × 0.999 ≈ 0.9985, which is 99.85%.

questions.q: Azure RBAC role 'Reader' can:
questions.why: The Azure Reader role is read-only. It can view resources but cannot create, delete or assign roles.

questions.q: Case: Production DB must not be deleted accidentally on Azure. Use:
questions.why: A CanNotDelete resource lock stops the production DB from being deleted accidentally. Tags, DNS and Front Door don't protect against deletion.

questions.q: Case: Need RPO 5 min, RTO 1 h, moderate budget. Strategy?
options: Pilot light/warm standby with continuous replication
questions.why: RPO 5 min and RTO 1 h at moderate budget fit pilot light or warm standby with continuous replication. Weekly backups are too slow and active-active is too costly.

questions.q: Case: Developer leaked an access key. First step?
questions.why: Deactivate and rotate the leaked key first to stop misuse. Deleting only the repo leaves the key valid.

questions.q: Case: 1.5M function calls × 0.2 s × 0.5 GB = GB-seconds?
Case: Need 1,000 usable IPs in an Azure subnet. Smallest prefix?
questions.why: Azure reserves 5 addresses per subnet. A /23 gives 512 − 5 = 507, which is too few, while a /22 gives 1,024 − 5 = 1,019. So /22 is the smallest that gives 1,000.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.why: ExpressRoute, Direct Connect and Cloud Interconnect are the Azure, AWS and Google dedicated private links. The other sets mix unrelated services.

questions.q: Why are Google service-account key files discouraged?
options: They're long-lived secrets that can leak; attached service accounts give short-lived credentials
questions.why: Service-account key files are long-lived secrets that can leak. A service account attached to the resource provides short-lived credentials, so no key file exists.

questions.q: Which choice best improves reliability AND keeps cost moderate for a regional web app?
questions.why: Multi-AZ autoscaling with a reserved baseline improves reliability while keeping cost moderate. A single huge VM or spot-only database is fragile, and five regions active-active is costly.

corp-conduct.title: Code of Conduct, ethics, anti-bribery and data privacy
corp-conduct.description: Chapter-by-chapter workplace integrity: a company Code of Conduct, ethical decision-making, insider trading and fair competition, anti-bribery law, and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The Code of Conduct in practice
courses.summary: What a Code of Conduct is for and how to apply it to conflicts of interest, gifts and hospitality, confidentiality and company assets, and speaking up without fear.
outcomes: Learners can explain the purpose and typical contents of a Code of Conduct
Learners can spot and disclose a conflict of interest
Learners can apply gift and hospitality rules
Learners can protect confidential information and company assets
Learners can raise a concern through the right channel

lessons.title: Why a Code exists and what it covers

scenes.text: On joining day, Varun is asked to read and accept a 30-page Code of Conduct. He scrolls to the end and clicks 'I agree'.
A week later a vendor offers him a free phone. He has no idea whether that's allowed.
His buddy says: 'The Code answers exactly this. Let's read the parts that matter.'

steps.title: What a Code of Conduct is
steps.body: A **Code of Conduct** is a company's written set of rules and values about how employees must behave. It turns laws (bribery, harassment, data protection, competition, insider trading) and the company's values into **clear everyday rules**. Breaking it is usually **misconduct** and can lead to warnings, termination, and sometimes legal action.

steps.title: Typical contents
steps.body:
- Respect: anti-harassment (POSH), anti-discrimination, safety
- Conflicts of interest and outside work
- Gifts, hospitality and anti-bribery
- Confidential information, IP and data privacy
- Use of company assets, IT and social media
- Accurate books, records and reports
- Fair competition and insider trading
- Speak-up channels and non-retaliation

steps.title: Rules vs judgement
steps.body: No Code can list every situation. That is why most Codes give a **decision test**: Is it legal? Is it consistent with our policies and values? Would I be comfortable if it appeared in the newspaper or my manager saw it? If unsure — **ask before you act**.

steps.title: Solved example: Varun's phone
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Find the gifts section: gifts of more than nominal value from vendors are not allowed, and any gift during an active purchase decision is not allowed.
**Step 2:** A phone is not nominal, and the vendor is bidding for a contract Varun influences.
**Step 3:** Politely decline, and inform his manager/compliance as the Code requires.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the Code as 'legal small print' — it is the rulebook you will be judged by.
- Assuming 'everyone does it' is a defence — it never is.
- Thinking the Code stops at office hours — social media, side businesses and conduct with clients apply too.

activity.prompt: Order the quick decision test.
items: Does it follow our policies and Code?
Would I be comfortable if it became public?
If still unsure — ask before acting

options: Turns laws and values into everyday rules
quiz.why: A Code of Conduct turns laws and values into everyday rules. It does not replace the law, and it isn't optional reading.

quiz.q: Breaking the Code is usually treated as:
quiz.why: Breaking the Code is usually treated as misconduct and can lead to disciplinary action.

quiz.q: When unsure if something is allowed you should:
quiz.why: When unsure whether something is allowed, ask before acting. Doing it quickly or ignoring the doubt risks a breach.

quiz.q: Does the Code apply to your social-media posts about work?
quiz.why: Yes. Codes cover online conduct linked to work, including social-media posts about your employer, even if anonymous.
'Everyone does it' is not a defence, because common practice doesn't make something right or allowed.

scenes.text: Deepa is choosing a facilities vendor. One bidder is owned by her cousin.
Her cousin's price is actually the best. Can she just pick it?
She decides to disclose first.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A **conflict of interest** exists when your **personal interest** (or that of family or close friends) could influence — or **appear** to influence — your judgement on behalf of the company. Having a conflict is not always wrong; **hiding** it is.

steps.title: Common types
steps.body:
- Relatives or friends as vendors, customers or candidates
- Investments in suppliers, customers or competitors
- Second jobs, freelancing or a side business (moonlighting) that competes or uses company time/assets
- Board seats or advisory roles
- Romantic relationships with someone in your reporting line

steps.title: The three Ds
steps.body: **Disclose** in writing (to manager/compliance) → **Distance** yourself from the decision (recuse) → **Document** how it was managed.

steps.title: Solved example: Deepa
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Identify — cousin owns a bidder → actual conflict.
**Step 2:** Disclose in writing before evaluation.
**Step 3:** Recuse — another colleague evaluates and decides.
**Step 4:** If the cousin's firm wins on merit through an independent process, that can be acceptable — and it is documented.

steps.title: Solved example: weekend freelancing
steps.body:
**Case:** A developer builds apps on weekends for a client that is a competitor of his employer.
**Analysis:** competing business + risk of using confidential knowledge → conflict; most Codes require prior approval and would refuse. Building a personal non-competing app on own devices and time may be allowed after disclosure — check the contract and policy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'I didn't benefit, so no conflict' — the *appearance* matters too.
- Disclosing after the decision.
- Using company laptop or code for a side project.

activity.prompt: Conflict of interest?

items.text: Interviewing your sister for your team
Holding a large stake in a supplier you manage
Freelancing for a direct competitor
Owning a small index fund
Volunteering at an NGO on weekends with no business link
Dating someone who reports to you

quiz.q: The main problem with a conflict of interest is usually:
quiz.why: Having a conflict of interest is not itself the main problem; hiding it is. Disclosure lets it be managed.
The right order is disclose, distance yourself and document. Disclose first so the conflict can be managed, rather than deciding first.
Even an apparent conflict, with no actual benefit, should be disclosed, because the appearance alone damages trust.

quiz.q: Which is most likely a conflict?
quiz.why: Freelancing for a competitor competes with your employer, so it is likely a conflict. A diversified mutual fund, running and guitar are not.
Recusal means stepping away from the decision so someone independent can decide.

scenes.text: During Diwali, Neeraj receives a dry-fruit box from a vendor — and another vendor sends a smartwatch.
A third invites him to a weekend resort 'to discuss the roadmap'.
His company has a gift limit and a register. He checks each one.

steps.title: Why gifts are risky
steps.body: Gifts create a sense of **obligation**. Small courtesies build relationships; lavish ones can look like (or be) a bribe. So Codes set **value limits**, ban gifts **during tenders or decisions**, ban **cash and cash equivalents** (gift cards, vouchers), and require **registering** what you accept or decline.

steps.title: The usual test (GIFT)
steps.body:
- **G**enuine — a courtesy, not a payment for a decision?
- **I**ndependent — would it not affect your judgement?
- **F**ree of obligation — no expectation attached?
- **T**ransparent — would you be happy to record it in the register and tell your manager?

steps.title: Solved example: Neeraj's three offers
steps.body:
Assume policy limit ₹2,000 and register required.
**1) Dry-fruit box (~₹800), festival courtesy:** within limit, not during a tender → may accept; record it.
**2) Smartwatch (~₹15,000):** above limit → decline politely, or hand to compliance if return is impossible; record.
**3) Weekend resort 'meeting':** mostly leisure, high value → decline; offer an office meeting instead.

steps.title: Hospitality
steps.body: A modest business meal where business is genuinely discussed is usually fine. Red flags: family members invited, travel paid to leisure destinations, frequent expensive events, or offered during a decision.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Accepting an Amazon voucher because it 'isn't cash' — vouchers are cash equivalents.
- Splitting a big gift into smaller ones to stay under the limit.
- Forgetting the rules also apply when **you give** gifts to clients and officials.

activity.prompt: Using a ₹2,000 limit and a no-gifts-during-tender rule, decide.

items.text: ₹500 box of sweets at Diwali from a long-time supplier
₹5,000 gift card from a vendor
Branded notebook at a conference
Dinner offered by a bidder during an active tender
Free family holiday from a client

quiz.q: Gift cards and vouchers are usually treated as:
quiz.why: Gift cards and vouchers are usually treated as cash equivalents, with the same risk as cash.

quiz.q: Gifts during an active tender are:
quiz.why: Gifts during an active tender are typically banned because they look like attempts to influence the decision.

quiz.q: If you can't return an expensive gift, you should:
options: Hand it to compliance and record it
quiz.why: If you can't return an expensive gift, hand it to compliance and record it, for transparency. Keeping it quietly or passing it on is not acceptable.

quiz.q: Splitting a large gift into small ones:
quiz.why: Splitting a large gift into small ones circumvents the policy, since the same value falls under the same rule.
In the GIFT test, T stands for Transparent: would you be comfortable recording it openly?

lessons.title: Confidential information, assets and social media

scenes.text: Excited about launch day, Alisha posts a photo of her desk on LinkedIn.
In the background, her monitor shows a customer list and next quarter's pricing.
A colleague spots it within minutes.

steps.title: What is confidential
steps.body: Anything not public: customer and employee data, prices, contracts, product plans, source code, financial results before release, strategy decks, and vendor terms. It stays confidential **even after you leave** the company.

steps.title: Company assets
steps.body: Laptops, accounts, software licences, code, data, time and brand are company assets. Use them for work; limited personal use only if policy allows. Don't install unapproved software, copy data to personal drives or email, or use company code in personal projects.

steps.title: Solved example: Alisha's post
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Delete the post immediately.
**Step 2:** Report to her manager and security — a quick report lets them assess exposure.
**Step 3:** Learn: before posting from work, check screens, whiteboards and badges; use the company's social-media guidelines.

steps.title: Solved example: leaving the company
steps.body:
**Case:** Rohan resigns and wants to email his 'work samples' (client decks) to his Gmail.
**Analysis:** client decks are confidential company property → not allowed. He may keep his own offer letter, payslips and relieving letter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Pasting confidential text or code into public AI tools that are not approved by the company.
- Discussing deals loudly in cabs, trains and lifts.
- Speaking 'on behalf of the company' online without authorisation.

statements.s: Confidentiality duties end the day you resign.
Pasting client data into an unapproved public AI chatbot can breach policy and privacy law.
You may forward client decks to personal email before leaving.
Checking your screen before posting office photos is good practice.

quiz.why: Unreleased pricing is confidential because it is not public. A public website, office address and press release are already public.
After resigning, you may take only personal documents like payslips and a relieving letter. Source code, client lists and strategy decks belong to the company.

quiz.q: If you accidentally leak information you should:
quiz.why: If you accidentally leak information, remove it and report quickly. Fast reporting limits the damage, while hiding it or blaming IT makes it worse.

quiz.q: Using an unapproved public AI tool with confidential code is:
quiz.why: Putting confidential code into an unapproved public AI tool is a likely policy breach, because the data leaves controlled systems.

quiz.q: Speaking for the company on social media requires:
quiz.why: Speaking for the company on social media requires authorisation. Only authorised spokespeople may do so.

scenes.text: Kiran notices his manager asking the team to backdate invoices to hit the quarter's target.
He fears that if he speaks up, his rating will suffer.
He learns about the company's whistleblower hotline and its non-retaliation promise.

steps.title: Channels to speak up
steps.body:
- Your manager (if not involved) or skip-level manager
- HR, Legal or Compliance
- Ethics/whistleblower **hotline** (often anonymous, run by a third party)
- Audit Committee (for serious financial concerns)

In India, the **Companies Act, 2013 (Section 177)** requires listed companies and certain other companies to establish a **vigil mechanism** for directors and employees to report genuine concerns, with safeguards against victimisation.

steps.title: Non-retaliation
steps.body: Good Codes promise that **no one** who raises a concern **in good faith** will be punished — even if the concern turns out to be unfounded. Retaliation (demotion, bad rating, exclusion, threats) is itself serious misconduct.

steps.title: Solved example: how Kiran reports
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Note facts — which invoices, dates, who asked, emails.
**Step 2:** Manager is involved → use the hotline or Compliance.
**Step 3:** Report facts, not accusations: 'On 28 March, I was asked to change invoice dates from April to March for invoices 1021–1030.'
**Step 4:** Keep a copy of the report reference number; report any retaliation.

steps.title: Good faith
steps.body: Good faith means you honestly believe what you report. You don't need proof — that's the investigators' job. Deliberately false reports, however, are misconduct.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Investigating on your own (copying others' mailboxes, recording secretly) — may break rules and law.
- Waiting until it 'gets worse'.
- Going to the media first, before internal channels, without legal advice.

a.text: Your manager asks you to backdate invoices. What do you do?

choices.label: Do it — the manager is responsible
choices.feedback: You'd be participating in falsifying records.

choices.label: Decline politely and report via the hotline/Compliance

b.text: Auditors find the backdating. Your name is on the changes. 'I was told to' does not protect you. What now?

choices.label: Cooperate fully and explain truthfully
choices.feedback: Honesty now is the best remaining option.

c.text: A month later your manager excludes you from meetings. What do you do?

choices.label: Report possible retaliation to Compliance
Stay quiet
choices.feedback: Reporting retaliation protects you and others.

d.text: You face disciplinary action but your cooperation is noted. Lesson: refuse unethical instructions at the start.

e.text: Compliance investigates both the backdating and the retaliation. The process protects people who speak up in good faith.

quiz.q: Which Indian law requires a vigil mechanism for listed companies?
quiz.why: The Companies Act, 2013 (Section 177) requires a vigil mechanism for listed companies. The other Acts don't cover it.
Good faith means you honestly believe your concern is true. You don't need full proof or to be anonymous.

quiz.q: If your manager is involved, report to:
quiz.why: If your manager is involved, report to the hotline, HR or Compliance, which bypasses the conflict. Going to the same manager defeats the purpose.
Retaliation against someone who reports in good faith is serious misconduct. Non-retaliation protects good-faith reports even if they turn out wrong.
A good report contains specific facts, such as who, what, when and where, which help investigators. Guesses, rumours and insults do not.

questions.q: A Code of Conduct is best described as:
options: Everyday rules based on law and values
questions.why: A Code of Conduct is a set of everyday rules based on law and values. It is not optional advice or a marketing brochure.

questions.q: Gift cards from vendors are usually:
options: Treated like cash and not allowed
questions.why: Gift cards from vendors are treated like cash and are not allowed. They are cash equivalents.

questions.q: First step with a conflict of interest:
questions.why: The first step with a conflict of interest is to disclose it. Hiding or deciding on it yourself is wrong.

questions.q: Confidential duties after you leave:
questions.why: Confidentiality duties continue after you leave the company. They don't end or become public.

questions.q: A modest business lunch where work is discussed is:
questions.why: A modest business lunch where work is discussed is usually acceptable within policy as reasonable hospitality. It isn't automatically a bribe.

questions.q: Which is NOT a speak-up channel?
options: Posting accusations on social media first
questions.why: Posting accusations on social media first is not a speak-up channel. Use internal channels such as the hotline, compliance or a skip-level manager.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Having a conflict of interest is always a violation. Reason (R): Undisclosed conflicts damage trust.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: having a conflict is not a violation, but hiding it is, because undisclosed conflicts damage trust.

questions.q: Case: A vendor bidding for your contract sends a ₹10,000 watch. Best action?
questions.why: Decline or return a ₹10,000 watch, tell compliance and record it. It is over limit and comes from a vendor with an active bid.

questions.q: Using company laptop to build a startup app at night is:
options: Likely a misuse of assets and possible conflict
questions.why: Using a company laptop to build a startup app is likely a misuse of company assets and a possible conflict, with intellectual-property risk.

questions.q: Which statement about non-retaliation is correct?
options: Good-faith reports are protected even if unfounded
questions.why: Good-faith reports are protected even if they turn out to be unfounded. Good faith is the test, not proof.

questions.q: Case: You realise a photo you posted shows a confidential whiteboard. Order of actions?
questions.why: Delete the photo, report it to your manager or security, then learn from it. Waiting, leaving it or just editing the caption leaves the information exposed.

questions.q: Case: Your spouse joins a competitor in a senior role. What should you do?
options: Disclose to manager/compliance and agree safeguards
questions.why: Disclose to your manager or compliance and agree safeguards, because a spouse at a competitor is a potential conflict. Sharing plans or doing nothing is wrong.

questions.q: Which BEST fits the 'newspaper test'?
options: Would I be comfortable if this action were reported publicly?
questions.why: The newspaper test asks whether you'd be comfortable if the action were reported publicly. It is a transparency check.

questions.q: Case: Your manager asks you to change a delivery date in a report to show the project 'on time'. Which Code area is breached?
questions.why: Changing a delivery date to show the project 'on time' falsifies records, breaching the accurate books and records rules.

questions.q: Case: You suspect fraud by a director. Internal channels seem compromised. The most appropriate formal channel for listed companies is:
options: The vigil mechanism, including direct access to the Audit Committee chair in appropriate cases
questions.why: For a listed company, the vigil mechanism (Section 177) includes direct access to the Audit Committee chair in appropriate cases. Use this rather than a WhatsApp group or deleting evidence.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Ethical decision-making, insider trading and fair competition
courses.summary: Frameworks for hard choices, why good people rationalise bad decisions, India's insider trading rules, and competition law basics.
outcomes: Learners can apply three ethical lenses to a dilemma
Learners can name the fraud triangle and common rationalisations
Learners can explain UPSI, trading windows and designated persons
Learners can recognise cartel conduct and bid rigging

scenes.text: Two days before launch, QA lead Swati finds a rare bug that may expose some users' addresses.
Leadership wants to launch on time and 'patch later'.
Swati needs a structured way to argue her case.

steps.title: Lens 1: consequences
steps.body: Who is helped or harmed, how much, and how likely? Choose the option with the best overall outcome for **all** stakeholders, not just this quarter's numbers.

steps.title: Lens 2: duties and rights
steps.body: What do we owe people regardless of outcome? Duties to tell the truth, keep promises, obey law, respect privacy and consent. Some actions are wrong even if profitable.

steps.title: Lens 3: character
steps.body: What would a person of integrity do? What kind of professional and company do we want to be? If this became a habit, who would we become?

steps.title: Solved example: Swati's dilemma
steps.body:
**Consequences:** a data leak could harm users, invite regulatory penalties and destroy trust; a 1-week delay costs some revenue.
**Duties:** duty to protect users' personal data (and legal duty under data-protection law).
**Character:** a trustworthy company doesn't knowingly ship a privacy bug.
**Decision:** recommend delaying or launching with the affected feature disabled; document the risk in writing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using only one lens (usually short-term profit).
- Framing it as a false choice — look for a **third option** (e.g. launch without the risky feature).
- Not writing your concern down.

activity.prompt: Match each question to its lens.
pairs: Who is harmed and how much?
Are we breaking a promise or law?
What would a person of integrity do?
What's the best outcome for all stakeholders?

quiz.why: The consequences lens asks who is helped or harmed by a decision, looking at outcomes for stakeholders.

quiz.q: Which lens says some acts are wrong even if profitable?
quiz.why: The duties and rights lens says some acts are wrong even if profitable, because duty-based thinking looks at promises, rights and rules.
A 'third option' means looking beyond a false either/or to find creative alternatives.

quiz.q: Best practice when you raise an ethical risk:
quiz.why: When you raise an ethical risk, write it down. Documentation creates a record and shows you acted.

options: What would a person of integrity do?
quiz.why: The character lens asks what a person of integrity would do, which is the virtue question.

lessons.title: Why good people do bad things

scenes.text: Raj, a careful accountant, is in debt after a family illness.
He notices nobody checks small travel claims.
'I'll pay it back. The company owes me anyway,' he tells himself.

steps.title: The fraud triangle
steps.body:
Criminologist Donald Cressey's **fraud triangle** says three elements usually come together:
- **Pressure** (financial stress, targets)
- **Opportunity** (weak controls)
- **Rationalisation** (a story that makes it feel OK)

Companies reduce **opportunity** with controls; individuals guard against **rationalisation**.

steps.title: Common rationalisations
steps.body:
- 'I'll pay it back' (borrowing)
- 'Everyone does it'
- 'No one gets hurt'
- 'They underpay me, I deserve it'
- 'My boss told me to'
- 'It's a grey area'

steps.title: Solved example: break the triangle for Raj
steps.body:
**Pressure:** use the company's salary advance or employee assistance options; talk to HR confidentially.
**Opportunity:** the company introduces random audits of claims.
**Rationalisation:** Raj notices the phrase 'I'll pay it back' as a warning sign and stops.

steps.title: The slippery slope
steps.body: Big frauds usually start small: a rounded-up claim, a 'temporary' adjustment. Each step makes the next easier. The cheapest moment to stop is the first one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing 'I'm a good person, so I can't do wrong' — situations shape behaviour.
- Ignoring colleagues' pressure signals; good managers notice and offer support.

activity.prompt: Which side of the fraud triangle?

items.text: Huge personal loan EMIs
No one reviews expense claims under ₹5,000
'The company won't miss it'
Aggressive quarter-end sales target
One person both approves and pays vendors
'I'm only borrowing it'

quiz.q: The three sides of the fraud triangle are:
quiz.why: The fraud triangle has three sides: pressure, opportunity and rationalisation, from Cressey's model.

quiz.q: Companies mainly reduce which side with controls?
quiz.why: Companies mainly reduce opportunity with controls, since controls limit chances to commit fraud. Pressure and rationalisation are harder to remove.
'I'll pay it back' is a classic rationalisation, a story the person tells to justify wrongdoing.

quiz.q: Segregation of duties (one person approves, another pays) reduces:
quiz.why: Segregation of duties, where one person approves and another pays, reduces opportunity because fraud then needs collusion.

quiz.q: The cheapest time to stop a slippery slope is:
quiz.why: The cheapest time to stop a slippery slope is the first step, because each step makes the next easier.

scenes.text: Mohit, a finance analyst at a listed company, works on a confidential acquisition.
His friend asks, 'Should I buy your shares this month?'
Mohit remembers the insider trading rules.

steps.title: The rules
steps.body: In India, insider trading is governed by the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**. An **insider** must not trade in a listed company's securities while in possession of **Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)**, and must not **communicate** UPSI to others except for legitimate purposes or duties.

steps.title: What counts as UPSI
steps.body:
Information not generally available that is likely to materially affect the share price, ordinarily including:
- financial results
- dividends
- change in capital structure
- mergers, demergers, acquisitions, delistings, disposals and expansion
- changes in key managerial personnel

steps.title: Trading window and designated persons
steps.body: Companies maintain a list of **designated persons** (employees with access to UPSI) and close the **trading window** around results and big events. Designated persons need **pre-clearance** for trades above set thresholds and must follow rules such as a minimum holding period / no contra trade within 6 months.

steps.title: Solved example: Mohit's reply
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Is the acquisition UPSI? Yes — not public, price-sensitive.
**Step 2:** Can he tip his friend? No — communicating UPSI is prohibited; the friend trading would also be a violation.
**Step 3:** Reply: 'I can't discuss company matters or give stock tips.' He should also not trade himself until the information is public and the window reopens.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking it's fine to trade through a spouse or friend's account — still a violation.
- Hinting ('let's just say good things are coming') — still communicating UPSI.
- Trading the day results are released before they are actually public.

statements.s: Upcoming quarterly results not yet published are typically UPSI.
You may trade through your brother's account if you have UPSI.
A hint about a big upcoming deal can be communicating UPSI.
Trading windows close around results announcements.

quiz.q: Insider trading rules in India are issued by:
quiz.why: SEBI issues insider trading rules in India, in the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015.
UPSI stands for Unpublished Price Sensitive Information, meaning non-public information that could affect a share price.
A pending acquisition is ordinarily UPSI because it isn't public and is price-sensitive. A published report, address or public speech is already public.

quiz.q: Designated persons usually need what before trading?
quiz.why: Designated persons usually need pre-clearance before trading, above set thresholds.

quiz.q: Telling a friend to 'buy before next week' when you know of a deal is:
quiz.why: Telling a friend to 'buy before next week' when you know of a deal is communicating UPSI, or tipping, which is prohibited.

lessons.title: Fair competition: cartels and bid rigging

scenes.text: At an industry conference, a competitor's sales head says, 'Let's not undercut each other — keep prices above ₹500.'
Sales manager Arvind is tempted; the price war has hurt.
He remembers: this is exactly what competition law forbids.

steps.title: Competition Act, 2002
steps.body: India's **Competition Act, 2002**, enforced by the **Competition Commission of India (CCI)**, prohibits **anti-competitive agreements** and **abuse of dominant position**. Agreements between competitors that **fix prices**, **limit production or supply**, **share markets or customers**, or **rig bids** are presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition.

steps.title: Red flags in conversation
steps.body: Discussing with competitors: future prices, discounts, margins, bids, capacity plans, which customers or regions each will take, salary-fixing or no-poach deals. Even an informal 'understanding' over coffee can be an agreement.

steps.title: Solved example: Arvind's response
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Stop the conversation clearly: 'I can't discuss pricing with you.'
**Step 2:** Leave the discussion (visibly, if in a group).
**Step 3:** Write a note of what happened and report to Legal the same day.
**Why:** silent presence at a price-fixing talk can be treated as participation.

steps.title: Solved example: bid rigging
steps.body:
**Case:** Three suppliers agree that Supplier A will win a government tender; B and C submit higher 'cover bids'.
**Analysis:** bid rigging → prohibited cartel conduct; serious penalties for companies and individuals involved.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharing competitor-sensitive data through industry associations.
- Thinking 'we never signed anything' is a defence.
- Assuming competition law only matters for giant firms.

activity.prompt: Safe or risky with a competitor?

items.text: Discussing a public industry safety standard
Agreeing on next quarter's price floor
Agreeing not to bid for each other's customers
Chatting about cricket
Exchanging planned discount levels
Agreeing not to hire each other's staff

quiz.q: Indian competition law is enforced by:
quiz.why: The Competition Commission of India (CCI) enforces competition law in India.
Price-fixing between competitors is prohibited, as cartel conduct. It is not allowed even if informal.

quiz.q: Cover bids in a tender are a sign of:
quiz.why: Cover bids in a tender are a sign of bid rigging, as they create fake competition.

quiz.q: If a competitor raises prices at a meeting you should:
options: Object, leave and report to Legal
quiz.why: If a competitor raises prices at a meeting, object, leave and report to Legal. Silence can imply participation.
An unwritten understanding can be an 'agreement' under competition law. Informal arrangements count.

questions.q: The fraud triangle consists of:
questions.why: The fraud triangle has three sides: pressure, opportunity and rationalisation (Cressey).

questions.q: UPSI rules are issued by:
questions.why: SEBI issues the rules on UPSI and insider trading. RBI, CCI and MCA regulate other areas.

questions.q: Price-fixing is prohibited under:
questions.why: Price-fixing is prohibited under the Competition Act, 2002 as an anti-competitive agreement.

questions.q: Which is a rationalisation?
questions.why: 'No one gets hurt' is a rationalisation, a self-justifying story. Audit, segregation of duties and pre-clearance are controls.

questions.q: Which is NOT ordinarily UPSI?
questions.why: A published annual report is already public, so it isn't UPSI. A pending merger, unannounced dividend and upcoming results are.

questions.q: The 'duties' lens focuses on:
questions.why: The duties lens focuses on rights, promises and law, a deontological view, not only profit or speed.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Trading through a relative's account while holding UPSI is allowed. Reason (R): Only the insider's own account is regulated.
questions.why: Both are false: trading through a relative's account while holding UPSI is prohibited, since indirect trading counts, and regulation isn't limited to the insider's own account.

questions.q: A no-poach agreement between competitors is:
questions.why: A no-poach agreement between competitors is risky under competition law, because it is a form of market-sharing for labour.

questions.q: Segregation of duties mainly reduces:
questions.why: Segregation of duties mainly reduces opportunity, since no one person can commit and hide fraud alone.

questions.q: Case: A privacy bug before launch. The best 'third option' is:
options: Launch with the risky feature disabled and fix it
questions.why: Launching with the risky feature disabled and fixing it is a 'third option' that balances outcomes and duties. Hiding the bug or cancelling everything isn't.

questions.q: Case: At an association meeting, members begin sharing planned price rises. You should:
options: Object, ask for it to be minuted, leave, inform Legal
questions.why: Object, ask for it to be minuted, leave and inform Legal. Silence can imply participation, and leaving without telling anyone leaves the risk unreported.

questions.q: Case: A designated person sells shares one week after buying, during an open window. Likely issue?
questions.why: Selling shares one week after buying breaches the contra-trade restriction, a minimum holding period. Codes typically bar contra trades within 6 months.

questions.q: Case: A sales head under target pressure, weak approval controls, and says 'everyone pads numbers'. Which triangle sides are present?
questions.why: Target pressure is the pressure, weak approval controls the opportunity, and 'everyone pads numbers' the rationalisation. So all three sides are present.

questions.q: Which BEST describes why bid rigging harms society?
options: Buyers (often taxpayers) pay inflated prices while competition is faked
questions.why: Bid rigging harms society because buyers, often taxpayers, pay inflated prices while competition is faked.

questions.q: Case: You overhear UPSI in a lift and buy shares. Are you exempt because you are not an employee?
options: No — anyone in possession of UPSI can be an insider under the Regulations
questions.why: Under the Regulations, anyone in possession of UPSI can be an insider, not only employees. So overhearing UPSI and trading is not exempt.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Anti-bribery and anti-corruption
courses.summary: What bribery is, India's Prevention of Corruption Act (as amended in 2018) including corporate liability, global laws (UK Bribery Act, US FCPA), facilitation payments, third-party red flags and what to do when asked for a bribe.
outcomes: Learners can define bribery and 'undue advantage'
Learners can explain key provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act after 2018
Learners can compare the UK Bribery Act and US FCPA at a high level
Learners can spot third-party red flags
Learners can respond safely to a bribe request

scenes.text: A new warehouse is waiting for a fire safety approval. The file has been stuck for weeks.
A middleman tells logistics manager Imran, 'Pay ₹50,000 and it will move tomorrow.'
Imran pauses: is this just how things work — or a crime?

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: **Bribery** is offering, promising, giving, requesting or accepting **anything of value** (an 'undue advantage') to **improperly influence** someone in their duties. 'Anything of value' includes cash, gifts, jobs or internships for relatives, travel, loans, donations, discounts and favours.

steps.title: Both directions
steps.body:
- **Active bribery:** giving or offering.
- **Passive bribery:** requesting or accepting.
Both are wrong; many laws punish both.

steps.title: Solved example: Imran
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Is something of value offered? Yes — ₹50,000.
**Step 2:** To influence an official's duty? Yes — to speed approval.
**Step 3:** Through a middleman? Doesn't matter — paying via a third party is still bribery.
**Conclusion:** refuse, document, report to Legal/Compliance.

steps.title: Solved example: the internship
steps.body:
**Case:** A customs official asks if your company can 'give an internship' to his nephew while your consignment is pending.
**Analysis:** a job for a relative is something of value, and timing links it to a decision → bribery risk. Decline and report; hire only through normal processes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'it's not a bribe if it's small' — size doesn't change the nature.
- Thinking non-cash favours don't count.
- Thinking 'the agent did it, not us' protects the company.

activity.prompt: Something of value that could be a bribe?

items.text: Cash to an inspector to skip a check
Paying the official government fee with a receipt
Job for an official's son during a licence review
A donation to an official's family trust to win a contract
Paying a vendor's invoice for delivered goods

quiz.why: Bribery requires value that is meant to improperly influence someone's duties. It need not be in writing, in cash or over a set amount.

quiz.q: An internship for an official's relative can be:
quiz.why: An internship for an official's relative is something of value, since benefits to relatives count as bribery value.
Paying through a middleman is still bribery, as indirect payments count.
Passive bribery means requesting or accepting a bribe, the receiving side. Giving is active bribery.
A small bribe is still a bribe, because size doesn't matter.

lessons.title: India's Prevention of Corruption Act after 2018

scenes.text: A construction firm's agent bribes a municipal officer to win a contract. The directors say they never knew.
Under the amended law, the company itself can be prosecuted.
Its only defence: proving it had adequate anti-bribery procedures.

steps.title: The law
steps.body:
The **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (PCA)** was significantly **amended in 2018**. It deals with bribery of **public servants**. Key points:
- A public servant who obtains or accepts an undue advantage for improper performance commits an offence (punishable with imprisonment of **3 to 7 years** and fine).
- **Giving** or promising an undue advantage to a public servant is a **specific offence** (punishable with imprisonment up to **7 years**, or fine, or both).

steps.title: Corporate liability (Section 9)
steps.body: A **commercial organisation** commits an offence if **any person associated with it** (employee, agent, consultant, distributor) gives or promises an undue advantage to a public servant intending to **obtain or retain business or an advantage** for it. It is punishable with fine. **Defence:** the organisation proves it had **adequate procedures** in place, in line with guidelines, to prevent such conduct. Where the offence is committed with the consent or connivance of a director, manager or officer, that person can also be punished.

steps.title: Coercion exception
steps.body: The giving-bribe offence does not apply to a person who was **compelled** to give an undue advantage, **provided** they report the matter to the law-enforcement authority or investigating agency **within 7 days** of giving it. This protects genuine victims of extortion who report promptly.

steps.title: Solved example: does Section 9 apply?
steps.body:
**Facts:** agent (associated person) bribes municipal officer (public servant) to win a contract (business advantage).
**Step 1:** Associated person? ✔ **Step 2:** Undue advantage to public servant? ✔ **Step 3:** To obtain business? ✔
**Result:** company liable unless it proves adequate procedures (due diligence on agents, training, contract clauses, monitoring, reporting lines).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Directors didn't know, so the company is safe' — Section 9 is about the organisation's procedures.
- Assuming the PCA covers private-to-private bribery — it targets public servants; private bribery is still banned by company Codes and may break other laws (e.g. UK Bribery Act if it applies).

This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Elements of 'adequate procedures' a company should have
items: Top-level commitment and a clear anti-bribery policy
Risk assessment of countries, deals and third parties
Due diligence on agents, distributors and consultants
Anti-bribery clauses and audit rights in contracts

quiz.q: The PCA was significantly amended in:
quiz.why: The Prevention of Corruption Act was significantly amended in 2018.
Section 9 makes commercial organisations liable for bribes paid on their behalf, as a corporate offence.
The company's defence under Section 9 is proving it had adequate procedures to prevent bribery. Small amounts or an agent's fault don't help.

quiz.q: A person compelled to pay must report within:
quiz.why: A person compelled to pay a bribe must report within 7 days to be protected.

quiz.q: Maximum imprisonment for giving a bribe under the amended PCA:
quiz.why: Under the amended PCA, giving a bribe can be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years.

scenes.text: An Indian IT company wins work in another country through a subsidiary with UK and US links.
A local official asks for a small 'processing fee' with no receipt.
Which laws apply now?

steps.title: UK Bribery Act 2010
steps.body: Covers bribing and being bribed, bribery of **foreign public officials**, and a corporate offence of **failure to prevent bribery** (defence: adequate procedures). It covers **private-sector** bribery too and gives **no exemption for facilitation payments**. It can apply to organisations that carry on business in the UK.

steps.title: US FCPA 1977
steps.body: The **Foreign Corrupt Practices Act** prohibits bribing **foreign officials** to obtain or retain business, and has **books-and-records and internal-controls** rules for companies listed in the US. It has a narrow exception for 'routine governmental action' facilitating payments — but many companies ban them anyway, and other laws (UK, India) don't allow them.

steps.title: Facilitation payments
steps.body: Small unofficial payments to speed up routine actions (e.g. stamping a visa or releasing goods). Because Indian law and the UK Act give no exemption, most global Codes **ban them completely**. The exception is **duress**: if you face a threat to life, liberty or safety, pay to stay safe and **report immediately** afterwards.

steps.title: Solved example: the 'processing fee'
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Is it an official fee with a receipt? No → unofficial payment.
**Step 2:** Is there a threat to safety? No → no duress.
**Step 3:** Decline politely: 'Our policy doesn't allow unofficial payments; I'm happy to pay any official fee with a receipt.'
**Step 4:** Report to Compliance; escalate delays through official channels.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only the law of the country where it happens applies — several laws can apply at once.
- Recording a bribe as 'consultancy' — that also breaks books-and-records rules.

activity.prompt: Match the law to its feature.
pairs: Corporate 'failure to prevent' offence; covers private bribery
Bribe-giving offence and commercial organisation liability
Small unofficial payment to speed routine action
Threat to safety — pay, then report immediately

quiz.q: Which law has no exemption for facilitation payments?
quiz.why: The UK Bribery Act has no exemption for facilitation payments, so they are illegal there.
The FCPA's accounting provisions are the books-and-records and internal controls requirements, alongside its anti-bribery provisions.

quiz.q: Under duress (threat to safety) you should:
quiz.why: Under duress, such as a threat to your safety, stay safe first and report immediately afterwards. Record the payment accurately instead of hiding it.

quiz.q: Recording a bribe as consultancy breaches:
quiz.why: Recording a bribe as consultancy creates a false record, which breaches books-and-records rules.

quiz.q: Can more than one country's law apply to the same bribe?
quiz.why: Yes. More than one country's law can apply to the same bribe, because anti-bribery laws have extraterritorial reach.

lessons.title: Third parties, red flags and saying no

scenes.text: A consultant promises to 'guarantee' a government licence for a 20% success fee, payable in cash to an account abroad.
Compliance analyst Leela runs due diligence.
Red flags pile up.

steps.title: Third-party red flags
steps.body:
- Unusually high commission or success fee
- Payment in cash, to third parties, or to offshore accounts
- Close family or business ties to officials
- Refusal to sign anti-bribery clauses or allow audits
- Vague services ('liaison', 'facilitation') with no deliverables
- Recommended by the official who will decide
- Requests for split invoices or round-number advances

steps.title: Due diligence steps
steps.body: 1) Identify ownership and beneficial owners. 2) Check sanctions and adverse media. 3) Verify qualifications and actual services. 4) Benchmark the fee. 5) Add contract clauses (anti-bribery, audit, termination). 6) Monitor invoices and activity.

steps.title: Solved example: Leela's review
steps.body:
Red flags found: 20% success fee (high), cash/offshore payment, 'guarantee' of a government decision, vague services.
**Decision:** reject the consultant; document reasons; brief the business team on lawful ways to pursue the licence.

steps.title: How to say no
steps.body:
- 'Our company has a strict no-bribes policy — I can't do that.'
- 'I'm happy to pay any official fee with a receipt.'
- 'Let me check with our compliance team.'
Then report the request the same day.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Don't ask, don't tell' with agents — wilful blindness does not protect you.
- Approving invoices for 'misc services' without proof of work.

a.text: A government officer hints that your tender 'will be easier' if you hire his recommended consultant. What do you do?

choices.label: Hire the consultant quickly
choices.feedback: Recommended by the decision-maker = red flag.

choices.label: Thank him, say you'll follow your process, and report to Compliance

b.text: The consultant asks for 15% in cash 'for expenses'. What now?

choices.label: Stop, refuse payment and report everything to Compliance
Pay and record as 'consultancy'

c.text: Compliance documents the approach, and the bid proceeds on merit. You protected yourself and the company.

d.text: An investigation later uncovers the payment. The company faces prosecution and you face personal liability. Lesson: red flags mean stop.

quiz.q: Which is a third-party red flag?
options: Payment to an offshore account in cash
quiz.why: A payment to an offshore account in cash is an unusual payment route, so it is a third-party red flag. A standard fee with invoice and clear deliverables isn't.
Wilful blindness, deliberately not knowing an agent's methods, doesn't protect you. It is not innocence.

quiz.q: A consultant recommended by the deciding official is:
quiz.why: A consultant recommended by the deciding official is a red flag, as they could be a conduit for a bribe.
Due diligence includes checking beneficial owners and sanctions, so you know who you deal with. Trusting a reference or website isn't enough.

quiz.q: After refusing a bribe request you should:
quiz.why: After refusing a bribe request, report it the same day. Prompt reporting protects you and the company.

questions.q: Bribery includes offering:
options: Anything of value to improperly influence
questions.why: Bribery includes offering anything of value to improperly influence, not just cash or large sums. It applies to private parties too.

questions.q: Facilitation payments under most global Codes are:
questions.why: Facilitation payments are banned under most global Codes, even small ones to speed up routine actions.

questions.q: Which Indian law covers bribery of public servants?
questions.why: The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 covers bribery of public servants in India.

questions.q: Section 9 PCA defence:
questions.why: The Section 9 PCA defence is adequate procedures. An agent acting alone or a small amount doesn't excuse the company.

questions.q: Which law has a 'failure to prevent bribery' corporate offence?
questions.why: The UK Bribery Act 2010 has a 'failure to prevent bribery' corporate offence (Section 7).

questions.q: A job for an official's relative during a pending decision is:
questions.why: A job for an official's relative during a pending decision is a bribery risk, as it is value given to a relative.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A company can be liable for a bribe paid by its agent. Reason (R): Under PCA Section 9, 'associated persons' include agents.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: Section 9 treats a company as liable for bribes by 'associated persons', which include agents.

questions.q: A person compelled to pay a bribe is protected if they report to law enforcement within:
questions.why: A person compelled to pay a bribe is protected if they report to law enforcement within 7 days.

questions.q: FCPA applies mainly to bribery of:
questions.why: The FCPA applies mainly to bribery of foreign officials. It doesn't focus on employees or private suppliers.

questions.q: Which is NOT a red flag?
options: Market-rate fee with clear deliverables and audit rights
questions.why: A market-rate fee with clear deliverables and audit rights is a normal arrangement. Ties to officials, vague 'liaison' services and cash requests are red flags.

questions.q: Case: A border guard threatens to detain your driver unless paid ₹2,000. The driver pays. What next?
options: Report immediately and record it accurately as a duress payment
questions.why: Safety comes first, so the driver may pay under duress. Then report immediately and record it accurately as a duress payment, not as fuel.

questions.q: Case: A consultant asks to split one invoice into five smaller ones under the approval limit. This suggests:
questions.why: Splitting one invoice into five smaller ones under the approval limit avoids controls, which is a classic red flag.

questions.q: Case: Bribe paid to a purchasing manager of a private company in India. Which is true?
options: PCA focuses on public servants, but company Codes ban it and other laws (e.g. UKBA) may apply
questions.why: The PCA focuses on public servants, but company Codes ban private bribery and other laws such as the UK Bribery Act may apply. So it is never fine.

questions.q: Which is the strongest evidence of 'adequate procedures'?
options: Risk assessment, due diligence, training, contract clauses, monitoring and reporting channels actually working
questions.why: Adequate procedures must be real and operating: risk assessment, due diligence, training, contract clauses, monitoring and working reporting channels. A speech, poster or unread PDF isn't enough.

questions.q: Case: An agent's success fee is 25% (market 3–5%), paid to a third-country account, and he refuses audit rights. Best decision?
questions.why: A 25% fee versus the 3–5% market rate, a third-country account and refused audit rights are multiple red flags, so reject the agent and document why.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Data privacy: India's DPDP Act, 2023 basics
courses.summary: Who's who under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; consent and notice; legitimate uses including employment; rights and duties of individuals; children's data; breaches, the Data Protection Board and penalties; and privacy habits at work.
outcomes: Learners can define Data Principal, Data Fiduciary, Data Processor and Consent Manager
Learners can describe valid consent and notice
Learners can list Data Principal rights and duties
Learners can explain obligations for children's data and breaches
Learners can apply privacy-by-default habits at work

scenes.text: Sunita's retail company is launching a loyalty app that collects names, phone numbers and purchase history.
A cloud vendor will store the data; a marketing agency will send offers.
Legal says, 'First, let's map who is who under the DPDP Act.'

steps.title: The Act
steps.body: The **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act)** is India's law on processing **digital personal data** — data about an identifiable individual that is collected digitally, or collected offline and later digitised. It also applies to processing **outside India** if it is connected to offering goods or services to people in India. Rules made under the Act (the DPDP Rules, 2025) set out details and phased timelines — always check the latest official notification for what is in force.

steps.title: Who is who
steps.body:
- **Data Principal:** the individual the data is about (for a child, includes the parent/lawful guardian).
- **Data Fiduciary:** decides the **purpose and means** of processing (like the 'controller').
- **Data Processor:** processes data **on behalf of** a Data Fiduciary.
- **Consent Manager:** a registered entity that lets Data Principals give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible platform.
- **Significant Data Fiduciary:** a fiduciary notified by government based on factors like volume and sensitivity of data and risk; has extra duties (e.g. a Data Protection Officer based in India, independent data audits, periodic impact assessments).

steps.title: What is outside
steps.body: The Act does not apply to personal data processed by an individual for **personal or domestic** purposes, or to personal data that the person themselves (or someone under a legal duty) has made **publicly available**.

steps.title: Solved example: map the loyalty app
steps.body:
**Customers** → Data Principals.
**Retail company** (decides why/how) → Data Fiduciary.
**Cloud vendor** and **marketing agency** (act on its instructions under contract) → Data Processors.
**Accountability:** the retail company stays responsible for compliance, including what its processors do.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the vendor is responsible — the Data Fiduciary remains accountable.
- Thinking paper records are always outside — they are covered once digitised.
- Treating 'publicly available' as 'anything on the internet' — the exemption is narrower (made public by the person or under law).

This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Match each party to its DPDP role.
pairs: A customer whose data is collected
The company deciding why data is collected
Cloud vendor storing data on the company's instructions
Large, high-risk fiduciary notified by government

quiz.q: The DPDP Act was enacted in:
quiz.why: The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act was enacted in 2023.

quiz.q: Who decides the purpose and means of processing?
quiz.why: The Data Fiduciary decides the purpose and means of processing. A processor acts on its behalf.

quiz.q: A payroll vendor processing salaries for your company is usually a:
quiz.why: A payroll vendor processing salaries for your company acts on its behalf, so it is a Data Processor.

quiz.q: Does the Act cover offline data that is later digitised?
quiz.why: Yes. The Act covers digital personal data, including offline data that is later digitised.

quiz.q: Who stays accountable for processors' actions?
quiz.why: The Data Fiduciary stays accountable for what its processors do with the data.

scenes.text: The app's signup screen has a pre-ticked box: 'I agree to share my data with partners for marketing.'
Legal flags it: 'That isn't valid consent under the DPDP Act.'
The team redesigns the screen.

steps.title: Valid consent
steps.body: Consent must be **free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous**, given by a **clear affirmative action**, and limited to the personal data **necessary** for the specified purpose. Pre-ticked boxes, bundled 'agree to everything' and making a service conditional on unrelated data fail this test. The Data Principal can **withdraw consent** at any time, and withdrawing must be **as easy as giving** it.

steps.title: Notice
steps.body: When asking for consent, the fiduciary must give a **notice** describing the personal data and purpose, how to exercise rights, and how to complain to the **Data Protection Board**. The Data Principal can access the notice in **English or any language in the Eighth Schedule** of the Constitution.

steps.title: Legitimate uses (no consent needed)
Solved example: redesign the screen
steps.body:
**Before:** pre-ticked 'share with partners'.
**After:** two separate unticked options: (1) 'Send me offers from this store' (2) 'Share my data with partner brands'. Account creation works even if both are unticked. A link to the notice, and 'Withdraw consent' is one tap in Settings.
**Result:** free, specific, affirmative, withdrawable ✔

steps.title: Solved example: HR data
steps.body:
**Case:** HR collects an employee's bank account to pay salary.
**Analysis:** employment purpose → legitimate use; consent not the basis. But HR must still protect it, use it only for that purpose and erase it when no longer needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'They accepted the T&Cs, so they consented to everything' — consent must be specific.
- Collecting extra fields 'just in case' — necessity applies.
- Making withdrawal hidden or slow.

activity.prompt: Valid consent design?

items.text: Unticked checkbox the user actively ticks
Pre-ticked marketing box
'Agree to all purposes or you can't use the app' for unrelated purposes
Separate opt-ins for each purpose
Withdrawal possible only by posting a letter
Notice available in Hindi and Tamil as well as English

quiz.q: Which is NOT a quality of valid consent?
quiz.why: Valid consent must be free, specific and informed, so bundling it with unrelated purposes is not valid.
Withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it (Section 6).

quiz.q: Processing employee bank details for salary relies on:
options: No basis needed and no duties
quiz.why: Processing employee bank details for salary relies on legitimate use for employment (Section 7), which doesn't need separate consent.

options: English or any Eighth Schedule language
quiz.why: A consent notice must be available in English or any Eighth Schedule language. This makes it accessible.
A pre-ticked box is not a clear affirmative action, so it is not valid consent.

lessons.title: Rights and duties of Data Principals

scenes.text: A customer emails: 'Tell me what data you hold about me, correct my address and delete my old orders.'
The support team has never handled such a request.
The privacy team explains the rights.

steps.title: Rights
steps.body:
- **Access information** (S.11): a summary of personal data processed and processing activities, and the identities of other fiduciaries/processors it was shared with.
- **Correction and erasure** (S.12): correct, complete, update, and erase data no longer needed (unless retention is required by law).
- **Grievance redressal** (S.13): a readily available mechanism; the fiduciary must respond within the period prescribed by the Rules. The person must use this before going to the Board.
- **Nominate** (S.14): nominate someone to exercise rights in case of death or incapacity.

steps.title: Duties of Data Principals (S.15)
steps.body: Comply with law; **not impersonate** another person; **not suppress material information** when giving data for official documents; **not file false or frivolous complaints**; give only verifiably authentic information when exercising correction. Breaching a duty can attract a penalty of up to **₹10,000**.

steps.title: Solved example: handle the email
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Verify identity securely (without over-collecting).
**Step 2:** Provide a summary of data held and with whom it was shared.
**Step 3:** Correct the address.
**Step 4:** Erase old orders **unless** law requires retention (e.g. tax/accounting records) — explain what was kept and why.
**Step 5:** Respond within the prescribed timeline and log the request.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring requests because 'there's no form'.
- Deleting records the law requires you to keep.
- Sending data to an unverified requester — that itself could be a breach.

activity.prompt: Match the request to the right.
pairs: 'What data do you have about me?'
'I want to complain about how you used my data'
'My spouse should manage this if I die'

quiz.q: Before approaching the Data Protection Board, a person should usually:
quiz.why: Before approaching the Data Protection Board, a person should usually use the fiduciary's grievance mechanism. Redressal there comes first.
Erasure may be refused when the law requires the data to be retained. Preference of the company isn't a reason.

quiz.q: Max penalty for breach of a Data Principal duty:
quiz.why: The maximum penalty for a Data Principal breaching their duties is ₹10,000, as set in the Schedule.
Filing a frivolous complaint is a breach of the Data Principal's duties (Section 15).

quiz.q: Before sharing data with a requester you should:
quiz.why: Before sharing data with a requester, verify their identity, so you don't disclose to impostors.

lessons.title: Children's data, breaches, the Board and penalties

scenes.text: Security detects that a misconfigured storage bucket exposed customer data — including some school students' records.
The incident manager wakes Legal. 'Who do we tell, and when?'
They open the breach playbook.

steps.title: Children's data (S.9)
steps.body: A **child** means a person who has **not completed 18 years**. Before processing a child's data the fiduciary must obtain **verifiable consent of the parent or lawful guardian**. It must **not** undertake processing likely to cause detrimental effect on a child's well-being, and must **not** do **tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising** directed at children (subject to exemptions the government may notify).

steps.title: Security and breach duties (S.8)
steps.body: Fiduciaries must take **reasonable security safeguards** to prevent breaches (including by processors). On a **personal data breach**, they must **intimate the Data Protection Board and each affected Data Principal** in the form and manner prescribed by the Rules. They must also **erase** data when the purpose is served or consent is withdrawn (unless law requires retention), and ensure data accuracy where it is used for decisions.

steps.title: Data Protection Board of India
steps.body: The **Board** inquires into breaches and complaints, can direct remedies and impose **monetary penalties**. Appeals go to the **Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT)**.

steps.title: Penalties (Schedule, maximum)
steps.body:
- Failure to take reasonable security safeguards: **up to ₹250 crore**
- Failure to notify the Board/affected persons of a breach: **up to ₹200 crore**
- Breach of children's data obligations: **up to ₹200 crore**
- Breach of Significant Data Fiduciary obligations: **up to ₹150 crore**
- Breach of Data Principal duties: **up to ₹10,000**
- Other breaches of the Act/Rules: **up to ₹50 crore**

steps.title: Solved example: the exposed bucket
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Contain — close public access, rotate keys, preserve logs.
**Step 2:** Assess — what data, whose, how many, children involved?
**Step 3:** Notify — the Data Protection Board and affected individuals as prescribed by the Rules (and CERT-In for cyber incidents under its directions).
**Step 4:** Remediate — fix configuration management, review processor contracts.
**Step 5:** Record lessons learned.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a 16-year-old as an adult user — under the DPDP Act a child is under 18.
- Waiting to 'be sure' before starting breach processes.
- Running targeted ads at teenagers.

This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Order the breach response.
items: Preserve evidence and assess the data affected
Notify the Data Protection Board and affected Data Principals as prescribed
Review lessons learned and update controls

quiz.q: Under the DPDP Act, a 'child' is a person under:
quiz.why: Under the DPDP Act, a child is a person who has not completed 18 years.

quiz.q: Max penalty for failing reasonable security safeguards:
quiz.why: Failing to take reasonable security safeguards can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore, the highest in the Schedule.

quiz.q: Appeals against the Board go to:
quiz.why: Appeals against the Data Protection Board's decisions go to TDSAT.

quiz.q: Targeted advertising directed at children is:
quiz.why: Targeted advertising directed at children is prohibited, subject to notified exemptions (Section 9).

quiz.q: On a personal data breach, the fiduciary must inform:
options: The Board and affected Data Principals
quiz.why: On a personal data breach, the fiduciary must inform the Board and the affected Data Principals (Section 8(6)).

scenes.text: A sales executive shares a spreadsheet of 2,000 customer phone numbers in a WhatsApp group to 'save time'.
One group member is a former employee.
The privacy lead runs a five-habit training the next week.

steps.title: Five habits
steps.body:
- **Minimise:** collect and share only what's needed.
- **Approved tools only:** no personal email, WhatsApp or public AI tools for personal data unless approved.
- **Need-to-know access:** don't share links to 'anyone with the link'.
- **Retain wisely:** delete when done, following retention schedules.
- **Report fast:** suspected leaks go to the privacy/security team immediately.

steps.title: Solved example: fix the WhatsApp share
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Delete the file from the group (for everyone) and ask members to delete copies.
**Step 2:** Report to the privacy team — it may be a personal data breach.
**Step 3:** Remove the former employee from work groups; review group membership.
**Step 4:** Share data through the approved CRM with access controls next time.

steps.title: Privacy by design
steps.body: When building anything new — app, survey, process — ask early: What data? Why? Who sees it? How long? How do people withdraw or delete?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Exporting full customer lists 'for analysis' when aggregated data would do.
- Leaving printed HR files on desks.

activity.prompt: My privacy habits this week
items: I checked who has access to my shared folders
I deleted personal-data exports I no longer need
I use only approved tools for customer and employee data
I know how to report a suspected data leak
I lock my screen when I step away

quiz.why: Data minimisation means collecting only what is needed. Collecting everything breaks the necessity principle.

quiz.q: Sharing customer lists in personal WhatsApp groups is:
options: A privacy risk and likely policy breach
quiz.why: Sharing customer lists in personal WhatsApp groups is a privacy risk and likely a policy breach, since it is an unapproved channel.
Privacy by design means considering privacy from the start, not adding it after launch.
Suspected leaks should be reported immediately, because speed limits the harm.

quiz.q: 'Anyone with the link' sharing for HR data is:
quiz.why: 'Anyone with the link' sharing for HR data is risky, because access should be on a need-to-know basis.

questions.q: The individual whom data is about is the:
questions.why: The individual the data is about is the Data Principal. The fiduciary decides how it's processed.

questions.q: DPDP Act year:
questions.why: The DPDP Act was passed in 2023.

questions.q: A child under the DPDP Act is under:
questions.why: A child under the DPDP Act is a person under 18.

questions.q: Valid consent must be:
questions.why: Valid consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous (Section 6). Pre-ticked or bundled consent isn't valid.

questions.q: Who hears appeals from the Data Protection Board?
questions.why: Appeals from the Data Protection Board go to TDSAT.

questions.q: Which is a Data Principal right?
questions.why: Correction and erasure are Data Principal rights (Section 12). Access to competitors' data or choosing the CEO are not.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Employers may process employees' data for employment purposes without consent. Reason (R): Employment is a legitimate use under Section 7.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: employment is a legitimate use under Section 7, so employers may process employees' data for employment purposes without consent.

questions.q: Max penalty for failing to notify a breach:
questions.why: The maximum penalty for failing to notify a breach is ₹200 crore, per the Schedule.

questions.q: A cloud vendor storing data for a bank is a:
questions.why: A cloud vendor storing data for a bank acts on the bank's behalf, so it is a Data Processor.

questions.q: Which is outside the Act?
options: Personal data processed for purely personal/domestic purposes
questions.why: Personal data processed for purely personal or domestic purposes is outside the Act. CRM data, payroll data and digitised forms are covered.

questions.q: Case: An ed-tech app wants to show behaviour-based ads to 15-year-olds with only the child's click-through consent. Problem?
options: Needs verifiable parental consent and targeted ads at children are prohibited
questions.why: Verifiable parental consent is needed for a child under 18, and targeted ads aimed at children are prohibited (Section 9). A child's click-through consent isn't enough.

questions.q: Case: A customer withdraws marketing consent. What must happen?
options: Stop processing for that purpose within a reasonable time and have processors stop too
questions.why: When consent is withdrawn, stop processing for that purpose within a reasonable time and have processors stop too. Legal retention, such as invoices, can still apply.

questions.q: Case: An employee posts a customer dataset to a public AI tool to 'clean it'. Which duties are at risk?
options: Reasonable security safeguards and purpose limitation
questions.why: Posting a customer dataset to a public AI tool puts reasonable security safeguards and purpose limitation at risk, since it is an uncontrolled disclosure.

questions.q: Which extra duties apply to a Significant Data Fiduciary?
options: DPO based in India, independent data audit, periodic impact assessment
questions.why: A Significant Data Fiduciary has extra duties: a DPO based in India, an independent data audit and periodic impact assessments (Section 10).

questions.q: Case: A user requests erasure of all data, including GST invoices from last year. Correct response?
options: Erase personal data not needed, but retain invoices required by law and explain this
questions.why: Erase personal data that is no longer needed, but retain invoices the law requires and explain this. Legal retention overrides erasure for those records.

courses.title: Conduct, ethics & privacy · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: One-page summaries of every chapter, a mixed scenario drill and a full mock test.
outcomes: Learners can recall the key rules of each chapter
Learners can choose the right action in mixed scenarios
Learners can score 80%+ in the mock test

scenes.text: Every employee must re-certify the Code this week.
Fatima builds a one-page summary to revise in ten minutes.

steps.title: Code of Conduct
steps.body:
- Ask before acting; 'everyone does it' is no defence
- Conflicts: disclose → distance → document
- Gifts: within limit, never during tenders, no cash/vouchers, register
- Confidentiality continues after exit
- Speak up in good faith; no retaliation; Companies Act 2013 S.177 vigil mechanism

steps.title: Ethics & markets
steps.body:
- Lenses: consequences, duties, character; look for a third option
- Fraud triangle: pressure, opportunity, rationalisation
- SEBI PIT Regulations 2015: no trading on or sharing UPSI; trading window; pre-clearance
- Competition Act 2002 (CCI): no price-fixing, market sharing, bid rigging

steps.title: Anti-bribery
steps.body:
- PCA 1988 (amended 2018): bribe-giving offence (up to 7 years); S.9 commercial organisation liability; defence = adequate procedures; compelled payer must report within 7 days
- UK Bribery Act 2010: failure to prevent; private bribery; no facilitation exemption
- US FCPA 1977: foreign officials + books & records

steps.title: DPDP Act 2023
steps.body:
- Roles: Principal, Fiduciary, Processor, Consent Manager, SDF
- Consent: free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, affirmative; easy withdrawal
- Legitimate uses incl. employment
- Rights: access, correction/erasure, grievance, nominate; duties (₹10,000)
- Children <18: verifiable parental consent; no tracking/targeted ads
- Penalties up to ₹250 cr (security), ₹200 cr (breach notice, children), ₹150 cr (SDF), ₹50 cr (others); Board → TDSAT

quiz.why: The vigil mechanism is under the Companies Act 2013, Section 177.
Under the PCA, giving a bribe can bring imprisonment up to 7 years.
A Significant Data Fiduciary breaching its obligations can face a penalty of up to ₹150 crore.
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) is the competition regulator.

scenes.text: Morning: a vendor gift. Noon: a competitor's price chat. Afternoon: a data request.
Evening: a friend asks about your company's results. Each needs a different rule.

steps.title: Drill 1
steps.body: **Vendor gift of ₹8,000 during tender** → decline, register, inform compliance.

steps.title: Drill 2
steps.body: **Competitor proposes 'price discipline'** → object, leave, report to Legal (Competition Act).

steps.title: Drill 3
steps.body: **Customer asks what data you hold** → verify identity, provide summary, log, respond in prescribed time (DPDP S.11).

steps.title: Drill 4
steps.body: **Friend asks if results will be good** → decline; it's UPSI (SEBI PIT Regulations).

steps.title: Drill 5
steps.body: **Official asks for 'speed money'** → refuse politely, offer official fee with receipt, report (PCA).

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the main rule.
pairs: Your cousin bids for your contract

quiz.why: Speed money, paid to make officials act faster, falls under anti-bribery law.
A tip about results before they are public is UPSI, so it falls under insider trading.
