options: Examine process, testing and safeguards that allowed it
questions.why: Systemic causes.

questions.q: Stand-down of a major incident occurs when:
options: Service is restored and confirmed stable
questions.why: Verify stability.

questions.q: Which metric best reflects major incident handling?
options: Time to declare and time to restore
questions.why: Outcome-oriented.

corp-itil-problem-change.title: ITIL 4 problem, change & service levels labs
corp-itil-problem-change.description: Problem management with root-cause analysis, change enablement, service level numericals and configuration management, taught through simulated tickets and calculations. Independent learning material; ITIL® is a registered trademark of PeopleCert/AXELOS and this course is not official or endorsed.

courses.title: Problem management & root-cause analysis
courses.summary: Turn recurring incidents into problems, find root causes with 5 Whys, fishbone and timelines, record known errors and workarounds. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Explain problem, known error and workaround
Run a 5 Whys and an Ishikawa analysis
Use trend data to identify problems proactively
Write a known-error record and a change proposal

lessons.title: Lab: Spot the problem in the incident trend

scenes.text: Anika, a service desk lead, notices 37 VPN incidents in six weeks, almost all logged between 09:00 and 09:30 on Mondays.
Each incident was closed with 'reconnected, working'. Nobody asked why it keeps happening.
She opens a problem record and links all 37 incidents to it.

steps.title: Three ITIL terms
steps.body:
- **Problem**: a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents.
- **Known error**: a problem that has been analysed but not yet resolved.
- **Workaround**: a solution that reduces or eliminates the impact of an incident or problem for which a full resolution is not yet available.

steps.title: Three phases
steps.body: Problem management runs in three phases: **problem identification** (trend analysis, recurring incidents, supplier info, major incidents), **problem control** (analysis, documenting workarounds and known errors) and **error control** (managing known errors and proposing permanent fixes via change enablement).

steps.title: Proactive vs reactive
steps.body: Reactive: open a problem after a major incident. Proactive: mine incident data for patterns *before* users suffer a big outage.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Closing each repeat incident as 'fixed' without linking it to a problem hides the real cost. Always link repeats.

activity.prompt: Which record or concept is each item?

items.text: Payroll app crashed for one user at 10:02
Unknown cause behind 37 Monday VPN drops
Root cause found: VPN concentrator licence pool too small; fix pending
Ask users to connect via the backup gateway vpn2.contoso.local
Printer on floor 3 jammed
Clear the browser cache to restore the portal until the patch ships

quiz.q: A problem that has been analysed but not yet resolved is a:
quiz.why: That is the ITIL 4 definition of a known error.

quiz.q: Which activity belongs to problem identification?
quiz.why: Identification looks for patterns, recurring incidents and other signals.

quiz.q: Why link repeat incidents to one problem record?
options: To raise their priority to P1
To show total impact and drive a permanent fix
quiz.why: Linked incidents quantify impact and justify investment.

options: Managing known errors and proposing permanent solutions
quiz.why: Error control manages known errors through to resolution.

scenes.text: Online checkout at an e-commerce firm failed for 40 minutes on Saturday.
Vikram, the problem manager, gathers the on-call engineer, a DBA and a developer and asks 'why?' five times.

steps.title: How 5 Whys works
steps.body: State the problem precisely, ask 'why did that happen?', and repeat on each answer until you reach a cause you can act on (often a process or design gap). Five is a guide, not a rule.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
- Checkout failed → the payment API timed out.
- Why? → DB connections were exhausted.
- Why? → a new report query held connections for minutes.
- Why? → it ran on the primary database, not the replica.
- Why? → the deployment checklist has no step to review query placement.

Action: add a query-review gate and route reports to the replica.

steps.title: Stop at blame? No
steps.body: 'Because Ravi made a mistake' is never a root cause. Ask why the system allowed the mistake.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body: Back every 'because' with evidence: logs, graphs, change records. Otherwise you are guessing.

activity.prompt: Put this 5 Whys chain in order from symptom to root cause.
items: A new report query held connections on the primary DB
No review step checks where heavy queries run

quiz.q: A good final 'why' usually points to:
options: A process or design gap you can fix
quiz.why: Actionable systemic causes prevent recurrence.

quiz.q: Each answer in a 5 Whys should be supported by:
options: Evidence such as logs and metrics
quiz.why: Evidence keeps the analysis honest.

options: No, stop when you reach an actionable root cause
quiz.why: Five is a heuristic.
Multi-cause problems need fishbone or fault-tree methods too.

scenes.text: Finance's month-end batch runs 6 hours late again.
The team draws a fishbone with categories: People, Process, Technology, Suppliers, Environment, Data.

steps.title: Why a fishbone
steps.body: An Ishikawa diagram puts the effect at the 'head' and groups possible causes along 'bones'. It stops the team fixating on the first idea and reveals multiple contributing causes.

steps.title: Example causes
steps.body:
- Technology: batch server at 95% CPU
- Process: jobs start in sequence, not parallel
- Data: duplicate records double the volume
- Suppliers: bank file arrives late

steps.title: Next step
steps.body: After brainstorming, test the top candidates with data. Then prioritise with a Pareto view: which few causes create most of the delay?

activity.prompt: Place each cause on the right bone.

items.text: Only one person knows how to restart the batch
Jobs run one after another with no parallelism
Batch server CPU at 95%
Bank statement file arrives 2 hours late
No runbook for failed jobs
Storage array latency spikes at 02:00

quiz.q: The head of a fishbone diagram holds:
quiz.why: Causes branch off toward the effect.
It structures brainstorming.

options: Fix all of them at once
Test candidates with data and prioritise
quiz.why: Validate before acting.

quiz.q: 'Only one person knows the restart' fits which category?
quiz.why: It is a skills/key-person risk.

scenes.text: Twelve incidents in a month: 'web app down' on WEB-APP02. Each time someone deleted logs and restarted.
You are the problem analyst. Find the root cause and get a permanent fix approved.

steps.title: Your job
steps.body: Investigate, separate clues from red herrings, identify the root cause, record the workaround and known error, and raise a change for the permanent fix.

steps.title: Closure note
steps.body: A good problem closure note states: root cause, evidence, workaround used, permanent fix (with change number) and how recurrence will be checked.

steps.title: Real world
steps.body: Most mature teams review open known errors weekly and measure 'repeat incidents avoided' to show the value of problem management.

ticket.short: Recurring outages of the customer portal on WEB-APP02
ticket.description: 12 incidents in 30 days. Users say 'portal is dead again'. Each time L1 cleared C:\inetpub\logs and restarted IIS. Works for a few days then fails again.

investigate.label: Check disk usage trend on WEB-APP02
investigate.reveal: C: grows about 3 GB per day and fills in 4–5 days.

investigate.label: Check which folder grows
investigate.reveal: C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles grows 2.8 GB/day; debug-level request logging was switched on during a test 6 weeks ago.

investigate.label: Review change records for WEB-APP02
investigate.reveal: CHG0031904 (6 weeks ago) enabled verbose logging for a test and was never reverted.

investigate.label: Ask users which browser they use
investigate.reveal: Chrome and Edge, mixed. Not relevant.

investigate.label: Check the network switch port
investigate.reveal: No errors on Gi1/0/14.

options: Verbose logging left on after a test, with no log rotation, fills drive C:
Users are using an old browser
diagnosis.why: Evidence: growth rate, folder and the unreverted change all point to logging without rotation.

resolution: Link all 12 incidents to the problem record
Document the workaround (archive old logs, restart app pool) in a known-error record
Raise a normal change to revert verbose logging and add a log retention policy
Implement after CAB approval and verify disk growth falls below 200 MB per day
Monitor for 30 days, then close the problem

closure.model: Root cause: verbose IIS logging enabled by CHG0031904 was never reverted, and no log retention existed, so C: filled every 4–5 days. Workaround (KE0001203): archive logs and recycle the app pool. Permanent fix via CHG0032550: logging reverted to standard and 14-day retention configured. Verification: disk growth now ~150 MB/day, no repeat incidents in 30 days. Lesson: test changes must include a back-out step.

quiz.q: Deleting logs each time was best described as a:
quiz.why: It restored service but did not remove the cause.

quiz.q: The permanent fix should go through:
quiz.why: Changes to live CIs need assessment and authorisation.

quiz.q: Which investigation item was a red herring?
quiz.why: Browsers had no link to disk filling.

quiz.q: When should the problem be closed?
options: After the fix is implemented and verified
As soon as the change is raised
quiz.why: Verify the fix removed recurrence.

questions.q: ITIL 4 defines a problem as:
options: A cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents
questions.why: Official meaning of problem.

questions.q: A workaround is:
options: A way to reduce impact until a full fix exists
questions.why: Workarounds reduce impact.

questions.q: Which phase records known errors and workarounds?
questions.why: Problem control analyses and documents.

questions.q: Trend analysis of incidents is an example of:
questions.why: Finding patterns before big failures.

questions.q: A root cause of 'engineer forgot' is weak because:
options: It blames a person and doesn't fix the system
questions.why: Look for the system gap.

questions.q: Fishbone diagrams help mostly by:
options: Grouping many potential causes by category
questions.why: Structured brainstorming.

questions.q: Which practice implements the permanent fix for a known error?
questions.why: Fixes are changes.

questions.q: A major incident was resolved by failover. What next?
options: Open a problem to find why the primary failed
questions.why: Major incidents trigger reactive problem management.

questions.q: Pareto analysis in RCA is used to:
options: Find the few causes behind most of the impact
questions.why: 80/20 prioritisation.

questions.q: A known error can stay open for a long time when:
options: The fix costs more than the impact justifies
questions.why: Risk is accepted with a workaround.

questions.q: Which evidence best confirms a root cause?
options: The fault can be reproduced and stops after removing the cause
questions.why: Reproduction plus removal is strong evidence.

questions.q: Twelve linked incidents cost 30 minutes each for 200 users. Total user-hours lost?

courses.title: Change enablement in practice
courses.summary: Standard, normal and emergency changes, risk assessment, change authority, schedules and post-implementation review through real change requests. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider.
outcomes: Classify standard, normal and emergency changes
Assess change risk and pick a change authority
Write a back-out plan
Run a post-implementation review

scenes.text: Leena, the change manager, has five requests on her desk before the weekend freeze.
Some are routine and pre-authorised; one is a live security hole.

steps.title: Three change types
steps.body:
- **Standard**: low-risk, pre-authorised, well understood, follows a documented procedure (e.g. add RAM to a VM via a template).
- **Normal**: must be scheduled, assessed and authorised following a process; the authority depends on risk.
- **Emergency**: must be implemented as soon as possible (e.g. fix an actively exploited vulnerability); assessment is expedited, often with a smaller authority.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.body: Change enablement maximises the number of successful changes by ensuring risks are properly assessed, changes are authorised and the change schedule is managed.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Using 'emergency' to dodge the process. Emergency changes should be rare and reviewed afterwards.

activity.prompt: Classify each change.

items.text: Reset a user's MFA using the documented procedure
Upgrade the core database cluster to a new major version
Patch an internet-facing VPN being actively exploited
Add a new monitor to an existing desk build
Migrate email to a new tenant
Revert a failed firewall rule blocking all payments

quiz.q: A pre-authorised, low-risk, repeatable change is:
quiz.why: Standard changes are pre-authorised.

options: Changes that must be implemented as soon as possible
quiz.why: Urgent need, e.g. active exploit.

options: A change authority appropriate to the risk
quiz.why: Authority scales with risk.

quiz.q: The main purpose of change enablement is to:
options: Maximise successful changes by managing risk
quiz.why: Enable, not block.

story.title: How risky is the SAN firmware?

scenes.text: A storage admin requests a SAN firmware update on the array that hosts 140 VMs.
Leena uses a simple risk score: likelihood × impact, each 1–5.

steps.title: Risk score
steps.body: Many organisations score risk = likelihood (1–5) × impact (1–5). Example bands: 1–6 low, 7–14 medium, 15–25 high. Higher scores need a more senior change authority (e.g. CAB).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: SAN firmware: likelihood of failure 3 (vendor notes known issues), impact 5 (140 VMs). Score 15 = high → CAB review, out-of-hours window, tested back-out.

steps.title: Lower the risk
steps.body: Pilot first, use a maintenance window, have a back-out plan and a tested backup, and staff the change with the right people.

activity.prompt: A change has likelihood 4 and impact 4. What is the risk score?

quiz.q: Likelihood 2, impact 3 gives a score of:
quiz.why: 2 × 3 = 6, low band in this model.

quiz.q: Which lowers change risk the most?
options: A tested back-out plan and pilot
quiz.why: Testing and back-out reduce impact.

quiz.q: A score of 20 in the example bands is:
quiz.why: 15–25 is high.

options: A CAB or senior change authority
quiz.why: Authority scales with risk.

Arjun must plan the renewal so nobody notices.

steps.title: A good change record has
steps.body:
- Description and reason
- CIs affected (from the CMDB)
- Risk and impact assessment
- Implementation plan with timings

- **Back-out plan**
- Communication plan

steps.title: Missing back-out
steps.body: A change without a tested back-out plan is a gamble. CABs often reject it.

steps.title: Before you start

quiz.why: Back-out restores the previous state.
CMDB shows CIs and relationships.

quiz.q: Why verify from an external client?
options: It proves users see the new certificate
quiz.why: Verification from the user viewpoint.

quiz.q: When should the CMDB be updated?
quiz.why: Records must match reality.

story.title: The firewall rule that broke payroll

scenes.text: A normal change tightened firewall rules on Saturday. Monday 09:10, payroll cannot reach the bank.
You must restore service, decide on back-out, and run the review.

steps.title: Failed change
steps.body: If a change causes an incident, restore service first (often via the back-out plan), then hold a post-implementation review (PIR) to learn why testing missed it.

steps.title: PIR questions
steps.body: Did the change meet its objectives? Was the risk assessed correctly? Were the right people involved? What will we change in the process?

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

ticket.short: Payroll can't send salary file to bank
ticket.description: Since this morning the bank upload just spins and then says connection failed. Salaries must go out today!!
worknotes: Linked change: CHG0032977 firewall hardening, implemented Sat 22:00

investigate.label: Check firewall deny logs for the payroll server 10.20.4.15
investigate.reveal: DENY tcp 10.20.4.15 -> 203.0.113.40:22 (SFTP) rule 'default-deny' since Sat 22:14.

investigate.label: Review the change's rule list
investigate.reveal: The old rule 'payroll-sftp-out' was removed as 'unused'; it is used only monthly.

investigate.label: Ask the user to clear browser cache
investigate.reveal: No change; the upload is a scheduled SFTP job.

investigate.label: Check bank status page
investigate.reveal: Bank reports all systems normal.

options: The firewall change removed a monthly-used SFTP rule
diagnosis.why: Deny logs began right after the change and show SFTP blocked.

resolution: Declare the link to CHG0032977 and inform the change manager
Restore the payroll SFTP rule via the emergency change / back-out procedure
Verify the bank upload succeeds
Communicate restoration to payroll
Schedule a post-implementation review of CHG0032977

closure.model: Cause: CHG0032977 removed firewall rule payroll-sftp-out believed unused; it is used monthly for the salary upload. Fix: rule restored via emergency change ECHG0004411 at 09:42. Verification: salary file uploaded and bank acknowledged at 09:51. PIR scheduled; action: usage review must cover at least 35 days of logs before removing rules.

quiz.q: First priority when a change breaks a service is:
quiz.why: Restore first, learn after.

options: Did the change meet objectives and what can we learn?
quiz.why: Learning-focused review.

quiz.q: Why was the rule thought unused?
options: Log review period was shorter than its monthly use
quiz.why: Too short an evidence window.

quiz.q: Restoring the rule under time pressure is typically handled as:
options: An emergency change or approved back-out
quiz.why: Still controlled, but expedited.

questions.q: Likelihood 5, impact 3 gives:
Which is the best candidate for a standard change?
options: Monthly OS patching via an approved, tested pipeline

questions.why: Avoid abuse.

questions.q: In DevOps pipelines, change authorisation can be:
options: Automated via policy and tests for low-risk changes
questions.why: ITIL 4 supports decentralised, automated authority.

questions.q: A change caused a P1. What happens after service is restored?
questions.why: Learn from failure.

questions.q: Which information comes from the CMDB during change assessment?
questions.why: Impact analysis uses relationships.

A change freeze during peak trading is mainly a control for:

courses.title: Service level management & numericals
courses.summary: SLAs, OLAs and underpinning contracts, availability, downtime budgets, MTTR/MTBF and SLA compliance calculations with worked numericals. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider.
outcomes: Distinguish SLA, OLA and underpinning contract
Calculate availability and allowed downtime
Compute MTBF, MTTR and SLA compliance
Spot the watermelon effect in reports

scenes.text: The HR department has an SLA: payroll app available 99.5% in business hours.
Inside IT, the database team has an OLA with the app team; the hosting vendor has a contract with IT.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **SLA**: a documented agreement between a service provider and a customer that identifies services required and expected service levels.
- **OLA**: an agreement between internal teams of the same provider that supports the SLA.
- **Underpinning contract**: an agreement with an external supplier that supports the SLA.

steps.title: Watermelon effect
steps.body: Green on the outside, red inside: all SLA metrics are met but users are unhappy. ITIL 4 encourages measuring outcomes and experience, not just technical uptime.

steps.title: Good SLAs
steps.body: Are simple, written in business language, linked to outcomes and reviewed regularly with the customer.

activity.prompt: Classify each agreement.

items.text: IT promises Sales: CRM 99.9% available 08:00–20:00
Network team promises app team: firewall changes in 2 days
Cloud vendor promises IT: 99.95% VM availability
Service desk promises staff: P3 resolved in 3 working days
DBA team promises app team: restore tests monthly

quiz.q: An agreement between two internal IT teams is a(n):
quiz.why: Operational level agreement.
Green outside, red inside.

quiz.q: A supplier's commitment to IT is a(n):
quiz.why: External supporting agreement.
Customers must understand them.

scenes.text: The payroll app's agreed service time in June was 22 business days × 10 hours = 220 hours.
It was down for 2 hours in total. Neha must report availability.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Availability % = (Agreed service time − Downtime) ÷ Agreed service time × 100**

Only downtime within agreed service time counts.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: (220 − 2) ÷ 220 × 100 = 99.09%. Target was 99.5%, so the SLA was **breached**. Allowed downtime at 99.5% = 220 × 0.005 = 1.1 hours = 66 minutes.

steps.title: Nines (24×7, 30-day month = 720 h)
steps.body:
- 99% → 7.2 h down allowed
- 99.9% → 43.2 min
- 99.99% → about 4.3 min

activity.prompt: Agreed service time is 500 hours; downtime was 1.5 hours. Availability to two decimals?

quiz.q: A 24×7 service in a 30-day month at 99.9% allows how much downtime?
Agreed time 220 h, downtime 2 h. Availability?

options: Usually does not count against the SLA
quiz.why: Measured over agreed service time.

lessons.title: Lab: MTBF, MTTR and SLA compliance

scenes.text: Over 30 days (720 h) the print server failed 4 times; total repair time was 8 hours.
The service owner wants MTBF and MTTR figures for the review.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **MTTR** (mean time to restore) = total downtime ÷ number of failures
- **MTBF** (mean time between failures) = total uptime ÷ number of failures
- **Availability** ≈ MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR)

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Downtime 8 h, 4 failures → MTTR = 2 h. Uptime 712 h → MTBF = 178 h. Availability = 178 ÷ 180 = 98.89%.

steps.title: SLA compliance
steps.body: 240 P3 tickets, 228 resolved within target → 228 ÷ 240 = 95%.

activity.prompt: A service ran 1,000 hours with 5 failures and 10 hours total downtime. What is MTBF (hours, based on uptime)?

quiz.q: Downtime 6 h over 3 failures gives MTTR:
Improving monitoring so failures are detected faster mainly reduces:
quiz.why: Faster detection shortens restore time.

scenes.text: Neha's report: availability 99.6% (target 99.5%), P2 compliance 92% (target 95%), CSAT 3.1/5.
The HR director says: 'Your report is green, but my team hates the app.'

steps.title: A real service review
steps.body: Discuss results against targets, customer experience, major incidents, trends, improvement actions and whether targets still fit business needs.

steps.title: Outcome metrics
steps.body: Add metrics that matter to the customer: time to run payroll, user-reported slowness, journey success rate.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

a.text: The HR director is frustrated: 'green report, unhappy users'. What do you do first?

choices.label: Point out that availability met the SLA
choices.feedback: Technically true, but it ignores the customer's experience.

choices.label: Ask what specifically frustrates users and when

b.text: The director escalates to your CIO. You get a second chance: what now?

choices.label: Listen and gather specific pain points

c.text: Users say the app takes 40 seconds to load payslips every morning. It's 'up', just slow. What do you propose?

choices.label: Add a response-time measure (e.g. 95% of pages under 3 s) and open a problem on the slowness
choices.feedback: Excellent: outcome metric plus problem management.

choices.label: Tell users to come in earlier
choices.feedback: Shifts the burden to the customer.

end1.text: The SLA is revised, a problem record finds a missing DB index, load time drops to 2 s and CSAT rises to 4.2.

end2.text: Dissatisfaction grows and the customer starts looking at SaaS alternatives.

quiz.why: Measure what customers value.

quiz.q: Slowness that recurs daily should trigger:
quiz.why: Recurring degradation needs a cause.

options: Whether targets still fit business needs
quiz.why: Targets evolve.

questions.q: An agreement with an external supplier supporting an SLA is a(n):
questions.why: External support contract.

questions.q: Availability formula numerator is:
questions.why: Uptime within agreed time.

questions.q: 24×7 for 30 days at 99% allows:
Agreed 400 h, downtime 4 h. Availability?
MTTR for 12 h downtime over 4 failures:
Uptime 600 h, 3 failures. MTBF?
MTBF 199 h, MTTR 1 h. Availability?

questions.why: Green outside, red inside.

Two components in series, each 99% available. Combined availability?
Two redundant servers in parallel, each 99%. Combined (independent failures)?
Which metric best reflects user experience of a web service?

courses.title: Service configuration management & CMDB
courses.summary: Configuration items, relationships, CMDB data quality, discovery, audits and using service maps for impact analysis. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider.
outcomes: Define CI, CMDB and CMS
Model relationships for impact analysis
Measure and fix CMDB data quality
Use a service map during an incident

story.title: Is the coffee machine a CI?

scenes.text: A new CMDB owner, Farhan, is asked whether to record every mouse, coffee machine and licence.
He learns that CIs are components that need to be managed to deliver a service.

steps.title: Configuration item
steps.body: A **configuration item (CI)** is any component that needs to be managed in order to deliver an IT service: servers, applications, databases, network devices, cloud resources, contracts, even key documentation.

steps.title: CMDB
steps.body: A configuration management database stores CI records and their **relationships** (runs on, depends on, connects to). The value comes from relationships, not just the list.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Recording everything at maximum detail. Capture the CIs and attributes you will actually use for incidents, changes and audits.

activity.prompt: Would you manage this as a CI for the payroll service?

items.text: Payroll application PAY-APP
Database server SQL-PAY01
Vendor support contract for the payroll software
Office coffee machine
A user's mousepad
Load balancer LB-DMZ02

options: Any component that needs to be managed to deliver a service
quiz.why: Broad but purposeful.

quiz.q: The main value of a CMDB comes from:
quiz.why: Relationships enable impact analysis.

quiz.q: Can a contract be a CI?
options: Yes, if it must be managed to deliver the service
quiz.why: Documentation and contracts can be CIs.

quiz.q: Right level of CMDB detail is:
options: What you will use and can keep accurate
quiz.why: Accuracy beats volume.

scenes.text: A change wants to reboot SQL-PAY01. Farhan checks the service map.
Payslip portal → PAY-APP → SQL-PAY01 → SAN-02.

steps.title: Relationship types
steps.body: Typical: *depends on*, *runs on*, *hosted on*, *connected to*, *used by*. A service map shows the chain from business service down to infrastructure.

steps.title: Impact analysis
steps.body: Rebooting SQL-PAY01 impacts PAY-APP and therefore the payslip portal and the HR self-service service. Users and SLAs attached to those services must be considered.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

activity.prompt: Order the dependency chain from business service down to storage.

quiz.q: If SAN-02 fails, which is affected?
options: Everything above it in the chain
quiz.why: Dependencies propagate upwards.

options: Impact analysis for incidents and changes
quiz.why: They show what depends on what.
It links two CIs.

scenes.text: Discovery found 1,200 servers; the CMDB lists 1,350. Who are the 150 ghosts?
Farhan measures accuracy and completeness.

steps.title: Quality measures
steps.body:
- **Accuracy**: records that match reality ÷ records checked
- **Completeness**: real CIs present in CMDB ÷ real CIs discovered
- **Currency**: how recently records were verified

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Audit sample of 200 records, 184 correct → accuracy 92%.

steps.title: Keep it true
steps.body: Use automated discovery, update CIs as part of change closure, and assign CI owners.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – CMDB during an outage

scenes.text: The customer portal is down. Three changes happened last night on different CIs.
The service map shows which of them sit on the portal's dependency chain.

steps.title: Use the map
steps.body: In an incident, check recent changes on CIs in the affected service's dependency chain first. Changes elsewhere are usually red herrings.

steps.title: Real world
steps.body: Industry post-incident studies repeatedly find that a large share of outages follow a change, so 'what changed?' is the first question.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

ticket.description: Customers get 'Bad Gateway' since about 06:30. Phones ringing nonstop.
worknotes: Changes last night: CHG0033001 printer driver update (floor 2), CHG0033002 TLS cipher change on LB-DMZ02, CHG0033003 HR app patch

investigate.label: Open the service map for PORTAL-WEB
investigate.reveal: PORTAL-WEB → LB-DMZ02 → APP-POOL-3 → SQL-CUST01.

investigate.label: Check LB-DMZ02 logs
investigate.reveal: 'SSL handshake failed with upstream 10.30.2.11:8443: no shared cipher' since 06:28.

investigate.label: Review the printer driver change
investigate.reveal: Floor-2 printers only; not on the portal chain.

investigate.label: Review the HR app patch
investigate.reveal: HR-APP is not related to the portal.

options: TLS cipher change on LB-DMZ02 broke upstream handshakes
diagnosis.why: It is the only change on the dependency chain and logs match.

resolution: Link the incident to CHG0033002
Back out the cipher change per its back-out plan
Verify the portal returns 200 and handshakes succeed
Update stakeholders
Open a problem/PIR on cipher compatibility testing

closure.model: Cause: CHG0033002 removed ciphers still required by the upstream app pool, causing TLS handshake failures (502). Fix: change backed out at 07:05. Verification: portal returning 200, no handshake errors for 30 min. Follow-up: PIR and app servers to be upgraded to support modern ciphers before retrying.

quiz.why: Focus on the chain.
